<P style="line-height:14.4px; margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><I>As used in this annual report, we refer to TransCommunity Financial Corporation as &#147;TransCommunity,&#148; Bank of Powhatan, N.A. as &#147;Bank of Powhatan,&#148; Bank of Goochland, N.A. as &#147;Bank of Goochland,&#148; Bank of Louisa, N.A. as &#147;Bank of Louisa,&#148;, and Bank of Rockbridge as &#147;Bank of Rockbridge&#148;.</I></P>
<P style="line-height:14.4px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.4px; margin:0px" align=center><B>PART I</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.4px; margin:0px" align=center><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:17.067px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-17.067px" align=justify><B>Item 1.</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.4px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:60px" align=justify><B>Business</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>General</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>TransCommunity Financial Corporation (&#147;TransCommunity&#148; or the &#147;Company&#148;) is a financial holding company headquartered in Richmond, Virginia. &nbsp;TransCommunity was formed in March 2001, principally in response to perceived opportunities resulting from the takeover in recent years of a number of Virginia-based banks by national and regional banking institutions. &nbsp;TransCommunity, through its four banking subsidiaries, Bank of Powhatan, Bank of Goochland, Bank of Louisa and Bank of Rockbridge (collectively, the &#147;banks&#148;), operates a community banking business in Central Virginia west and north of the greater Richmond metropolitan area. &nbsp;Bank of Powhatan, with one office in Powhatan County, opened for business in March 2000. &nbsp;TransCommunity became the holding company for Bank of Powhatan in August 2001, through a statutory share exchange transaction. &nbsp;Bank of Goochland, with two offices in Goochland County, opened for business in November 2002. &nbsp;Bank of Louisa, with one office in Louisa County, was originally established as a branch office of the Bank of Powhatan, and was &#147;spun off&#148; as a separately-chartered bank in April 2004. &nbsp;Bank of Rockbridge was opened in December of 2006.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, TransCommunity had total assets of $198.4 million, total loans net of the allowance for loan losses of $149.3 million, total deposits of $165.0 million and total stockholders&#146; equity of $30.6 million. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>TransCommunity&#146;s headquarters are located at 4235 Innslake Drive, Glen Allen, Virginia.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B>Recent Developments</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>In January 2007, our Board of Directors voted unanimously to consolidate our four existing bank charters into a single legal entity. &nbsp;The new consolidated bank will continue to do business under the names of the existing subsidiary banks. &nbsp;M. Andrew McLean, currently the president of the Company&#146;s Bank of Goochland subsidiary, will serve as president of the consolidated bank, and the current Board of Directors of the Company will serve as the Board of Directors of the bank. &nbsp;We are currently working through the consolidation process and expect to complete the consolidation process prior to the end of the third quarter of 2007. &nbsp;We believe that this consolidation of our bank charters will result in significantly lowered operating expenses, and can be achieved without impacting the local decision-making processes that are at the heart of our business model.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Our Growth Strategy</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Our goal is to provide superior, long-term returns to our shareholders by building a significant community banking franchise in Virginia. &nbsp;Virginia is dominated by large, out-of-state banks, which have expanded their market presence in Virginia primarily by acquiring Virginia-domiciled institutions. &nbsp;We intend to target underserved or over-consolidated markets in Virginia and to enter those markets through one of the following strategies:</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:99px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol"><B><I>&#183;</I></B></FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:99px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman"><B><I>Strategic De Novo Banks</I></B></FONT>. &nbsp;We have developed substantial knowledge and expertise in organizing <I>de novo</I> banks. &nbsp;To date, we have opened four <I>de novo</I> banks. &nbsp;We believe that there are significant operational and economic benefits to establishing new independent banks that outweigh the associated costs. &nbsp;While our banks are still relatively new, they have demonstrated that they can produce attractive margins and can reach operating profitability in a reasonable period of time. &nbsp;Bank of Powhatan reached operating profitability in its first two years, and Bank of Goochland reached operating profitability in 20 months. &nbsp;Bank of Louisa, which was spun off in 2004, became profitable in 2006. &nbsp;We may add additional <I>de novo</I> banks in attractive markets where we can hire experienced management teams. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:99px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol"><B><I>&#183;</I></B></FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:99px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman"><B><I>Opportunistic Acquisitions.</I></B></FONT> While Virginia is dominated by large, out-of-state banks, there are over 70 banking institutions headquartered in Virginia that have less than $250 million in assets. &nbsp;We believe that many of these smaller banks will seek to merge with companies that have the infrastructure in place to handle the growing back-office and regulatory burden faced by smaller institutions. &nbsp;TransCommunity&#146;s decentralized decision-making structure and approach should be attractive to the management, board of directors, employees and shareholders of such companies. &nbsp;We believe these factors will make TransCommunity a competitive acquirer. &nbsp;Our acquisition strategy will be opportunistic and is intended to augment our <I>de novo</I> bank strategy.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:99px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol"><B><I>&#183;</I></B></FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:99px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman"><B><I>Selective De Novo Branching.</I></B></FONT> &nbsp;To date we have organized four <I>de novo</I> banks, but only the Bank of Goochland has established a branch office. &nbsp;The Bank of Powhatan is actively evaluating its options for a new branch office in Powhatan County. &nbsp;As we grow, we will consider opportunities to establish new branches to leverage the brand awareness developed by our banks and to provide added convenience to our customers. &nbsp;In some cases, we may establish branches that operate under a separate name with a &#147;doing business as&#148; designation. &nbsp;For example, the Bank of Louisa operated under that name, but as a branch of the Bank of Powhatan, before Bank of Louisa was chartered as a separate bank.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B>Our Operating Strategy &#150; Common Operating Platform</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Under our business model, we seek to lower our operating costs and improve operating efficiencies by centralizing at the holding company many &#147;back room&#148; operations functions that do not routinely touch the customer. &nbsp;We refer to this basket of shared support services as our Common Operating Platform. &nbsp;Information technology, telephone and data services, item processing and website management are examples of the services that our holding company has routinely provided. &nbsp;Generally, we can provide these services at lower cost on a &#147;bulk buying&#148; basis.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>3</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>In addition, managing the delivery of these services from the holding company allows our subsidiary bank managers to devote more time to serving customers. &nbsp;In November, 2006, the Company&#146;s Board of Directors voted to expand the range of services provided under our Common Operating Platform to include deposit operations, loan administration and accounting. &nbsp;We believe that the addition of these additional services to our Common Operating Platform will serve to further reduce our operating costs as well as improve the quality of the support services provided to our banks.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Our Banks</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Bank of Powhatan.</I></B><I> </I>&nbsp;Bank of Powhatan commenced its banking operations in March 2000. &nbsp;In March 2001, the bank relocated to a permanent, newly-constructed facility located on the north side of U.S. Route 60, the major east-west highway in Powhatan County. &nbsp;Powhatan County is a suburb of Richmond and is experiencing significant growth in population. &nbsp;From 2000 to 2006, Powhatan Country&#146;s population grew 20.1%. &nbsp;The Powhatan County deposit market grew 231% or $126 million from June 2000 to June 2006, according to the latest report from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (the &#147;FDIC&#148;). &nbsp;The bank is evaluating opening a branch office in Powhatan County serving a highly desirable area, which includes a zip code that has one of the highest average household incomes in the greater Richmond metropolitan area.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, Bank of Powhatan had $70.7 million in total assets, total loans net of the allowance for loan losses of $57.0 million and $60.9 million of total deposits which represents a 27.2% market share in deposits versus 0% in 2000.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Bank of Goochland. &nbsp;</I></B>Bank of Goochland opened in November 2002. &nbsp;Goochland County is contiguous to Powhatan County but separated by the James River west of Richmond and a 45-minute drive from Charlottesville. &nbsp;Bank of Goochland initially conducted business from its present branch office facility at historic Goochland Courthouse, which serves the western portion of the Goochland market. &nbsp;Bank of Goochland&#146;s main office, which was opened in October 2003, is located in Centerville, on U. S. Route 250, a heavily-traveled route used by Goochland Country residents in their commute to and from work in the Richmond area. &nbsp;The location is six miles west of Innsbrook (where TransCommunity is headquartered), a significant business community in western Henrico Country. &nbsp;Goochland County has experienced a 17.4% population growth from 2000 to 2006. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
The deposits in Goochland County grew 89% or by $67.9 million from June 30, 2000 to June 30, 2006, according to the latest report from the FDIC.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, Bank of Goochland had $87.6 million in total assets, total loans net of the allowance for loan losses of $70.2 million and $77.5 million of total deposits which represents a market share of 53.8% versus 0% on June 30, 2002.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Bank of Louisa.</I></B> &nbsp;Bank of Louisa opened its first office in July 2003, in the Town of Louisa, as a branch of the Bank of Powhatan. &nbsp;Louisa County is contiguous to Goochland County&#146;s northern boundary and just east of Charlottesville. &nbsp;In April 2004, Bank of Louisa was spun off as a separately-chartered bank subsidiary of TransCommunity. &nbsp;Concurrent with its opening, Bank of Louisa purchased the assets and assumed the deposits of the Louisa branch of Bank of Powhatan. &nbsp;The permanent main office for Bank of Louisa, located in the town of Louisa, opened in April 2005. &nbsp;Louisa County has experienced 18% population growth from 2000 to 2006. &nbsp;Deposits in Louisa County grew 30% or $91 million from June 30, 2000 to June 30, 2006, according to the latest report from the FDIC.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, Bank of Louisa had $31.0 million in total assets, total loans net of the allowance for loan losses of $21.8 million and $26.0 million of total deposits which represents a market share of 9.8%. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Bank of Rockbridge. &nbsp;</I></B>The Bank of Rockbridge opened in December 2006. &nbsp;The central valley area including Rockbridge and the City of Lexington area grew 5.3% in population between 2000 and 2006. &nbsp;Deposits in Rockbridge County grew 55% or $170 million during this same time to $480 million, according to the latest report from the FDIC.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B>Lending Activities</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>General</I>.</B> &nbsp;Each of our subsidiary banks emphasizes a range of lending activities, including real estate, commercial, and consumer loans to individuals, small businesses and professional firms located in central Virginia. &nbsp;Each bank has its own loan underwriting authority exercised by its president and loan committee. &nbsp;We have developed a common set of loan underwriting standards for use by each of our banks which vary by type of loan, as described below. &nbsp;Each of our banks seeks to underwrite loans in accordance with these internal underwriting guidelines, as well as applicable regulatory supervisory limits. &nbsp;We do not maintain a loan committee at the holding company level. &nbsp;We believe that local lending authority allows us to be more responsive than our regional and national competitors.</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Since loans typically provide higher interest yields than other types of interest-earning assets, we seek to invest a substantial percentage of our earning assets in the loan portfolios of our subsidiary banks. &nbsp;We believe we have a competitive market advantage over larger national and regional banking institutions because we provide borrowers with a wide variety of lending products in the range of approximately $250,000 to $1.5 million that these larger banks may not want to offer because of the size or characteristics of the loan, or may not be able to deliver as expeditiously as we can. &nbsp;At December 31, 2006, we had total loans of $151.4 million, representing 80.6% of our earning assets.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Each of our banks seeks to maintain a diversified loan portfolio and to limit the amount of loans to any single client. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2006, the 25 largest client relationships at the Bank of Powhatan represented $12.8 million, or 22.1% of its loan portfolio. &nbsp;At the same date, Bank of Goochland reported loans totaling $41.8 million, or 58.8% of its portfolio, to its 25 largest borrowers. &nbsp;Bank of Louisa reported loans totaling $15.8 million to its largest 25 borrowers, which represented 71.5% of its total portfolio at December 31, 2006.<I> </I>As our banks continue to grow and mature, we expect that these concentrations will decrease as a percentage of total loans.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>4</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Regardless of the purpose of an individual loan, each of our banks seeks to obtain a security interest in real estate whenever possible, in addition to any other collateral available, in order to increase the likelihood of the ultimate repayment of the loan. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Loans Secured by Real Estate</I>.</B> &nbsp;At December 31, 2006, loans secured by real estate represented 73.3% of the loans in our consolidated portfolio. &nbsp;Real estate lending by our banks generally consists of commercial real estate loans, construction and development loans, and residential and home equity loans. &nbsp;Interest rates for all categories of real estate loans may be fixed or adjustable, with adjustable-rate loans predominating. &nbsp;In addition to interest, we generally charge an origination fee on each loan. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Real estate loans originated by our banks are subject to the same risks as other loans and are particularly sensitive to fluctuations in the value of real estate. &nbsp;While real estate market values in the central Virginia market have risen strongly during the past decade, fluctuations in the value of real estate, as well as other factors arising after a loan has been made, could negatively affect a borrower&#146;s cash flow, creditworthiness and ability to repay the loan.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Commercial Real Estate Loans</I>.</B> &nbsp;At December 31, 2006, commercial real estate loans totaled $60.6 million or 40.0% of our consolidated loan portfolio. &nbsp;These loans generally have rate terms of five years or less, although payments may be structured on a longer amortization basis. &nbsp;Each of our banks evaluates every borrower on an individual basis and attempts to determine the business risks and credit profile of each borrower. &nbsp;We also generally require that a borrower&#146;s cash flow be at least 115% of monthly debt service obligations. &nbsp;In order to insure secondary sources of payment and liquidity to support loan requests, we typically review personal financial statements of all principal owners and require their personal guarantees.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Construction and Development Real Estate Loans</I>.</B> &nbsp;Each of our banks offers residential and commercial construction loans to builders and developers as well as to consumers who wish to build their own homes. &nbsp;None of our banks makes loans in this category on a fixed-rate basis, and as of December 31, 2006, all loans in this category were adjustable rate loans. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2006, a total of $21.3 million, or approximately 14.1% of our consolidated loan portfolio consisted of construction and development real estate loans. &nbsp;The duration of our construction and development loans does not normally exceed 24 months. &nbsp;Construction and development loans generally carry a higher degree of risk than long-term financing of existing properties because repayment depends on the ultimate completion of the project and usually the sale of the property. &nbsp;Specific risks include:</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:75px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:75px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Cost overruns</FONT></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:75px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:75px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Mismanaged construction</FONT></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:75px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:75px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Inferior or improper construction techniques</FONT></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:75px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:75px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Economic changes or downturns during construction</FONT></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:75px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:75px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">A downturn in the real estate market</FONT></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:75px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:75px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Rising interest rates which may prevent sale of the property</FONT></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; padding-left:75px; text-indent:-24px; font-family:Symbol" align=justify><FONT FACE="Symbol">&#183;</FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:75px" align=justify><FONT FACE="Times New Roman">Failure to sell completed projects in a timely manner</FONT></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>We attempt to reduce the risk associated with construction and development loans by obtaining personal guarantees where possible and by keeping the loan-to-value ratio of the completed project at or below 80% for commercial loans and 85% for consumer loans.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Residential Real Estate Loans and Home Equity Loans</I></B><I>. &nbsp;</I>None of our banks originates traditional long- term residential mortgages, but each of our banks does issue second mortgage residential loans and home equity lines of credit. &nbsp;With respect to home equity lines of credit, our policy is to limit extensions of credit to 90% of the available equity in each property. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2006, a total of $29.0 million, or 19.2%, of our consolidated loan portfolio consisted of residential mortgage loans and home equity lines of credit. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Commercial Business Loans</I></B><I>.</I> &nbsp;Each of our banks makes loans for commercial purposes in various lines of business, including manufacturing, service industry and professional service areas. &nbsp;We also offer small business loans utilizing government enhancements such as the Small Business Administration&#146;s (&#147;SBA&#148;) 7(a) program and 504 program, which loans are partially guaranteed by the government, thereby reducing their risk. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2006, a total of $31.3 million, or 20.7%, of our consolidated loan portfolio consisted of commercial business loans. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Consumer Loans.</I></B> &nbsp;Each of our banks makes loans to individuals for personal and household purposes, including secured and unsecured installment loans and revolving lines of credit. &nbsp;Consumer loans are underwritten based on the borrower&#146;s income, current debt level, past credit history, and the availability and value of collateral. &nbsp;Consumer loans are both fixed and variable, with negotiable terms. &nbsp;Our installment loans typically amortize over periods not exceeding 60 months. &nbsp;Each of our banks offer consumer loans with a single maturity date when a specific source of repayment is available. &nbsp;Typically, each of our banks requires monthly payments of interest and a portion of the principal on revolving loan products. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2006, a total of $8.7 million, or 5.8%, of our consolidated loan portfolio consisted of loans to consumers. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Loan Approval.</I></B> &nbsp;Certain credit risks are inherent in making loans. &nbsp;These include prepayment risks, risks resulting from uncertainties in the future value of collateral, risks resulting from changes in economic and industry conditions and risks inherent in dealing with individual borrowers. &nbsp;Each of our banks attempts to mitigate repayment risks by adhering to internal credit policies and procedures. &nbsp;These policies and procedures, which are maintained by the holding company and are common to all of our subsidiary banks, include officer lending limits, a multi-layered loan approval process for larger loans, documentation examination, and follow-up procedures for any exceptions to credit policies. &nbsp;Each of our banks has a loan committee of its Board of Directors that is responsible for oversight of the lending function at that bank. &nbsp;When the amount of aggregate loans to a single borrower exceeds an individual officer&#146;s lending authority, the loan request will be considered by an officer with a higher lending authority or by the bank&#146;s loan committee. &nbsp;None of our banks makes any loans to (1) any director or officer of that bank, (2) any director or officer of any affiliate bank, or (3) any officer or director of the holding company, unless the loan is approved by the Board of Directors of the bank and is on terms not more favorable to such person than would be available to a person not affiliated with that bank.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>5</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Credit Administration and Loan Review.</I> &nbsp;</B>We maintain a continuous loan review system that is managed at the holding company level. &nbsp;Each of our banks also applies a consistent credit grading system to each loan, and we utilize an independent consultant to review the loan files annually on a test basis to confirm the grading of each loan. &nbsp;This independent consulting firm reports directly to the chairman of the Audit Committee of the holding company Board of Directors. &nbsp;We hold each loan officer responsible for the loans he or she makes, regardless of whether other individuals or committees joined in the approval. &nbsp;This responsibility continues until the loan is repaid or until the loan is formally assigned to another officer.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Lending Limits</I>.</B> &nbsp;The lending activities of each of our banks are subject to a variety of lending limits imposed by federal law. &nbsp;In general, each bank is subject to a legal limit on loans to a single borrower equal to 15% of that bank&#146;s capital and unimpaired surplus. &nbsp;This limit will increase or decrease as that bank&#146;s capital increases or decreases. &nbsp;Based on the capitalization of our banks at December 31, 2006, we currently self-impose loan limits of $1.1 million at Bank of Powhatan, $1.5 million at Bank of Goochland $700 thousand at Bank of Louisa and $1.1 million at the Bank of Rockbridge. &nbsp;Once we have completed the consolidation of our four existing bank charters, our new combined equity capital of $30.6 million will allow for a revised lending limit up to $4.6 million.</P>
<P style="margin-top:5.533px; margin-bottom:13.333px"><B>Deposit Services</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:5.533px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>We focus on customer service to attract and retain deposits. &nbsp;Each bank offers a full range of commercial and retail deposit services, including checking accounts, savings accounts, money market accounts and other time deposits of varying types. &nbsp;The principal source of deposits at each of our banks is the local, central Virginia market. Because of the historically low interest rate environment in the last four years, each of our banks has also been able to obtain a portion of its deposits from bank-to-bank deposits generated outside our local market at certain times. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2006, less than 2% of our consolidated deposits was from out of market sources. Deposit rates are reviewed regularly by senior management of each bank. We believe that the deposit rates we offer are competitive with those offered by other financial institutions in our market area. &nbsp;By focusing on core deposits, we believe we can continue to keep the overall cost of our deposits low and thereby benefit from wide net interest margins. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B>Competition</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Banks generally compete with other financial institutions through the selection of banking products and services offered, the pricing of services, the level of service provided, the convenience and availability of services, and the degree of expertise and the personal manner in which services are offered. &nbsp;Virginia law permits statewide branching by banks. &nbsp;Consequently, commercial banking in Virginia is highly competitive. &nbsp;Many large banking organizations, most of which are controlled by out-of-state holding companies, currently operate in the greater Richmond, Virginia metropolitan area, and our primary market area. &nbsp;As of June 30, 2006, the aggregate deposit market in the Commonwealth of Virginia amounted to approximately $173 billion, of which out-of-state banking institutions controlled approximately 64.5%of these deposits. &nbsp;In addition, competition between commercial banks and thrift institutions (savings institutions and credit unions) has intensified significantly in recent years with the elimination of many previous distinctions between the various types of financial institutions and the granting of expanded powers to thrift institutions in areas which previously had been the sole domain of commercial banks. &nbsp;Legislation enacted in recent years, together with other regulatory changes by the primary regulators of the various financial institutions, has resulted in the almost total elimination of practical distinctions between a commercial bank and a thrift institution. &nbsp;Consequently, competition among financial institutions of all types is largely unlimited with respect to legal ability and authority to provide most financial services. &nbsp;Furthermore, as a consequence of federal legislation, out-of-state banks not previously allowed to operate in Virginia are allowed to commence operations and compete in TransCommunity&#146;s primary market area. &nbsp;See &#147;Supervision and Regulation.&#148;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>TransCommunity faces competition from other banks, as well as thrift institutions, consumer finance companies, insurance companies and other institutions in our respective market areas. &nbsp;Some of these competitors are not subject to the same degree of regulation and restriction imposed upon the banks. &nbsp;Some of these competitors also have broader geographic markets and substantially greater resources and lending limits than our banks and offer certain services that our banks are not expected to provide in the near term. &nbsp;Such competitors may also be in a position to make more effective use of media advertising, support services and electronic technology than our banks can. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B>Employees </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, TransCommunity had 72 full-time equivalent (&#147;FTE&#148;) employees as compared to 110 FTEs at December 31, 2005.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Supervision and Regulation </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>General. &nbsp;</I></B>The following discussion sets forth some of the material elements of the regulatory framework applicable to bank holding companies and their subsidiaries and provides some specific information relevant to TransCommunity and the banks. &nbsp;Other laws and regulations that govern various aspects of the operations of banks and bank holding companies are not described herein, although violations of such laws and regulations could result in supervisory enforcement action against TransCommunity or a bank. &nbsp;The regulatory framework is intended primarily for the protection of depositors and the Federal Deposit Insurance Funds and not for the protection of security holders. &nbsp;To the extent that the following information describes statutory and regulatory provisions, it is qualified in its entirety by reference to the particular statutory and regulatory provisions. &nbsp;A change in applicable statutes, regulations or regulatory policy may have a material effect on TransCommunity and the banks.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Holding Company Regulation and Structure. &nbsp;</I></B>The Company is subject to regulation under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956 (&#147;BHCA&#148;) and the examination and reporting requirements of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Under the BHCA, a bank holding company may not directly or indirectly acquire ownership or control of more than 5% of the voting shares or substantially all of the assets of any bank or merge or consolidate with another bank holding company without the prior approval of the Federal Reserve Board. </P>

<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>The BHCA generally limits the activities of a bank holding company and its subsidiaries to that of banking, managing or controlling banks, or any other activity that is determined to be so closely related to banking or to managing or controlling banks that an exception is allowed for those activities. Under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (&#147;GLBA&#148;), however, qualifying bank holding companies may elect to be &#147;financial holding companies&#148; and to engage in a wider variety of activities. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><BR>
In the first quarter of 2004, we chose to be a financial holding company and, therefore, are permitted to engage, directly or through subsidiaries, in a wide variety of activities which are financial in nature or are incidental or complementary to a financial activity, in addition to all of the activities otherwise allowed to us. &nbsp;The additional activities permitted to us as a financial holding company (if we so determine to conduct them) include, among others, securities activities such as underwriting, dealing, and brokerage, investment and merchant banking, and insurance underwriting, sales and brokerage activities. &nbsp;The Company is also a registered bank holding company under the bank holding company laws of the Commonwealth of Virginia. Accordingly, the Company is also subject to regulation and supervision by the State Corporation Commission of Virginia. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The OCC conducts regular examinations of each nationally chartered bank, reviewing such matters as the adequacy of loan loss reserves, quality of loans and investments, management practices, compliance with laws, and other aspects of their operations. &nbsp;In addition to these regular examinations, each nationally charter bank must furnish the OCC with periodic reports containing a full and accurate statement of its affairs. </P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The state chartered Bank of Rockbridge will be regulated by the Virginia Bureau of Financial Institutions and the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond. &nbsp;These two regulators will provided similar oversight as outlined for our nationally charter banks.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>FDIC Insurance.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:144px" align=justify>&nbsp;The deposits of the Banks are insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (&#147;FDIC&#148;) up to the limits set forth under applicable law. The deposits of these banks are subject to the deposit insurance assessments of the Bank Insurance Fund (&#147;BIF&#148;) of the FDIC. &nbsp;The FDIC uses a risk-based assessment system for insured depository institutions that takes into account the risks attributable to different categories and concentrations of assets and liabilities. &nbsp;Depository institutions insured by the BIF are required to pay assessments for deposit insurance ranging from .043% to .05% of deposits. These rate schedules are subject to future adjustments by the FDIC. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>There are a number of obligations and restrictions imposed on bank holding companies and their depository institution subsidiaries by federal law and regulatory policy that are designed to reduce potential loss exposure to the depositors of such depository institutions and to the FDIC insurance funds in the event that the depository institution is insolvent or in danger of becoming insolvent. For example, under the policy of the Federal Reserve Board with respect to bank holding company operations, a bank holding company is required to commit resources to support its subsidiary depository institutions. In addition, the &#147;cross-guarantee&#148; provisions of federal law require insured depository institutions under common control to reimburse the FDIC for any loss suffered or reasonably anticipated by either the Savings Association Insurance Fund or the Bank Insurance Fund as a result of the default of a commonly controlled insured depository institution in danger of default. The FDIC may decline to enforce the cross-guarantee provision if it determines that a waiver is in the best interests of the deposit insurance funds. The FDIC&#146;s claim for reimbursement under the cross-guarantee provisions is superior to claims of shareholders of the insured depository institution or its holding company, but is subordinate to claims of depositors, secured creditors and nonaffiliated holders of subordinated debt of the commonly controlled insured depository institutions. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Interstate Banking. </I></B><I>&nbsp;</I>Federal law permits bank holding companies from any state to acquire banks and bank holding companies located in any other state, subject to certain conditions, including nation-wide and state-imposed concentration limits. Banks are also able to branch across state lines, provided certain conditions are met, including that applicable state laws expressly permit such interstate branching. Virginia has adopted legislation that permits branching across state lines, provided there is reciprocity with the state in which the out-of-state bank is located. After a bank has established branches in a state through an interstate merger transaction, the bank may establish and acquire additional branches at any location in the state where a bank headquartered in that state could have established or acquired branches under the applicable federal or state law. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Capital Requirements. &nbsp;</I></B>Banking regulatory agencies have issued risk-based and leverage capital guidelines applicable to banking organizations which they supervise. Under the risk-based capital guidelines of the federal regulatory agencies, the Company and the Banks are required to maintain a minimum ratio of total capital to risk-weighted assets of at least 8% and a minimum Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets of at least 4%. </P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><BR>
At least half of total capital is required to be composed of common equity, retained earnings and qualifying perpetual preferred stock, less certain intangibles and other adjustments (Tier 1 capital). The remainder (Tier 2 capital) may consist of a limited amount of subordinated debt and other qualifying debt (including certain hybrid capital instruments), and a limited amount of the loan loss reserve. As of December 31, 2006, each of our subsidiary banks were considered well capitalized under the regulatory guidelines of the FDIC. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s capital is discussed in greater detail under &#147;Management&#146;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operation &#150; Capital&#148; in Item 7 of this annual report and in Note 17 of the notes to consolidated financial statements under the caption Regulatory Matters, and those discussions are incorporated by reference herein. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>In addition, the Federal Reserve Board has established minimum leverage capital ratio guidelines for bank holding companies. These requirements provide for a minimum leverage ratio of tier 1 capital to adjusted average quarterly assets less certain amounts (&#147;leverage ratio&#148;) equal to 3% for bank holding companies that are rated a composite &#147;1&#148; and 4% for all other bank holding companies that meet certain criteria, including having the highest regulatory rating. &nbsp;The risk-based capital guidelines of the federal regulatory agencies explicitly identify concentrations of credit risk and the risk arising from non-traditional activities, as well as an institution&#146;s ability to manage these risks, as important factors to be taken into account by the agencies in assessing an institution&#146;s overall capital adequacy. The capital guidelines also provide that an institution&#146;s exposure to a decline in the economic value of its capital due to changes in interest rates be considered by the agency as a factor in evaluating a banking organization&#146;s capital adequacy. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>

<P style="margin:0px" align=center>7</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Limits on Dividends and Other Payments. &nbsp;</I></B>TransCommunity is a legal entity separate and distinct from its Banks. &nbsp;For the near-term, a significant portion of the revenues of TransCommunity will depend upon dividends or fees paid to TransCommunity by the Banks. &nbsp;Prior regulatory approval is required if the total of all dividends declared by a national bank in any calendar year will exceed the sum of that bank&#146;s net profits for that year and its retained net profits for the preceding two calendar years, less any required transfers to surplus.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Federal law also prohibits national banks from paying dividends that would be greater than the banks&#146; undivided profits after deducting statutory bad debts in excess of the banks&#146; allowance for loan losses. &nbsp;That means that each Bank must recover any start-up losses before it may pay a dividend to TransCommunity. &nbsp;As of December 31, 2006, the Bank of Powhatan and the Bank of Goochland were the only subsidiary banks that were in a position to pay a dividend to TransCommunity.</P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>In addition, TransCommunity and its subsidiaries are subject to various general regulatory policies and requirements relating to the payment of dividends, including the requirements to maintain adequate capital above regulatory minimums. &nbsp;The appropriate federal regulatory authority is authorized to determine, under certain circumstances relating to the financial condition of a bank or bank holding company, that the payment of dividends would be unsafe or unsound practice and to prohibit payment thereof. &nbsp;The appropriate federal regulatory authorities have indicated that paying dividends that deplete a bank&#146;s capital base to an inadequate level would be an unsound and unsafe banking practice and that banking organizations should generally pay dividends only out of current operating earnings. &nbsp;In addition, TransCommunity is subject to state laws that limit the amount of dividends it can pay to its shareholders. &nbsp;TransCommunity expects that these laws, regulations or policies will materially impact the ability of the Banks and, therefore, TransCommunity to pay dividends in the early years of operations. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Other Regulations. </I></B><I>&nbsp;</I>The Company and its subsidiary banks are also subject to certain other federal laws and regulations which directly impact operations of the Company:</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><I>USA Patriot Act</I>. &nbsp;The USA Patriot Act became effective in October 2001 and provides for the facilitation of information sharing among governmental entities and financial institutions for the purpose of combating terrorism and money laundering. Among other provisions, the USA Patriot Act permits financial institutions, upon providing notice to the United States Treasury, to share information with one another in order to better identify and report to the federal government concerning activities that may involve money laundering or terrorists&#146; activities. The USA Patriot Act is considered a significant banking law in terms of information disclosure regarding certain customer transactions. &nbsp;Certain provisions of the USA Patriot Act impose the obligation to establish anti-money laundering programs, including the development of a customer identification program, and the screening of all customers against any government lists of known or suspected terrorists. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:96px" align=justify><BR>
Although it does create a reporting obligation and compliance costs, the Company does not expect the USA Patriot Act to materially affect its products, services or other business activities. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><I>Community Reinvestment Act. &nbsp;</I>The banks are subject to the requirements of the Community Reinvestment Act (&#147;CRA&#148;). The CRA imposes on financial institutions an affirmative and ongoing obligation to meet the credit needs of their local communities, including low and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with the safe and sound operation of those institutions. A financial institution&#146;s efforts in meeting community credit needs are currently evaluated as part of the examination process pursuant to lending, investment and service tests. &nbsp;These factors are considered in evaluating mergers, acquisitions and applications to open a branch or facility, and an unsatisfactory rating can substantially delay or block a transaction. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><I>Reporting Terrorist Activities.</I> &nbsp;The Federal Bureau of Investigation (&#147;FBI&#148;) has sent, and will send, our banking regulatory agencies lists of the names of persons suspected of terrorist activities. Our subsidiary banks have been requested, and will be requested, to search their records for any relationships or transactions with persons on those lists. If the banks find any relationship or transactions, they must file a Suspicious Activity Report and contact the FBI. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (&#147;OFAC&#148;), which is a division of the Department of the Treasury, is responsible for helping to ensure that United States entities do not engage in transactions with &#147;enemies&#148; of the United States, as defined by various Executive Orders and Acts of Congress. OFAC has sent, and will send, our banking regulatory agencies lists of names of persons and organizations suspected of aiding, harboring or engaging in terrorist acts. If the banks find a name on any account, or wire transfer that is on an OFAC list, they must freeze such account, file a Suspicious Activity Report and notify the FBI. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><I>Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (&#147;SOX&#148;).</I> &nbsp;TransCommunity is subject to the periodic reporting requirements of the Securities and Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the &#147;Exchange Act&#148;), including the filing of annual, quarterly and other reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the &#147;SEC&#148;). &nbsp;As an Exchange Act reporting company, TransCommunity is directly affected by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (&#147;SOX&#148;), which is aimed at improving corporate governance and reporting procedures. &nbsp;TransCommunity believes it is in substantial compliance with applicable SEC and other rules and regulations implemented pursuant to SOX and intends to comply with any applicable rules and regulations implemented in the future. &nbsp;Because the stock of TransCommunity is not listed on any national securities exchange or quoted on the NASDAQ Market System, certain provisions of SOX, including Section 404, and the regulations adopted or to be adopted there under, do not currently apply to TransCommunity.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><I>Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 (&#147;GLBA&#148;). &nbsp;</I>The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Financial Modernization Act of 1999 (&#147;GLBA&#148;) was enacted on November 12, 1999, and became effective March 11, 2000. &nbsp;The GLBA enables bank holding companies to acquire insurance companies and securities firms and effectively repeals depression-era laws that prohibited the affiliation of banks and other financial services entities under a single holding company. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Bank holding companies and other types of financial services entities may elect to become financial holding companies under the GLBA. &nbsp;Financial holding companies are permitted to engage in activities considered financial in nature, as defined in GLBA, and may engage in a substantially broader range of activities than bank holding companies or banks. &nbsp;The GLBA enables financial holding companies to offer virtually any type of financial service, or services incident to financial services, including banking, securities underwriting, insurance underwriting and making merchant banking investments in commercial and financial companies. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>8</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify>The new financial services authorized by the GLBA also may be engaged in by a &quot;financial subsidiary&quot; of a national or state bank, with the exception of insurance or annuity underwriting, insurance company portfolio investments, real estate investment and development, and merchant banking, all of which must be conducted under the financial holding company. &nbsp;In addition, the GLBA allows insurers and other financial services companies to acquire banks; removes various restrictions that applied to bank holding company ownership of securities firms and mutual fund advisory companies; and establishes the overall regulatory structure applicable to bank holding companies that also engage in insurance and securities operations.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>To become a financial holding company, a bank holding company must provide notice to the Federal Reserve Board of its desire to become a financial holding company, and certify to the Federal Reserve Board that it and each of its bank subsidiaries is &quot;well-capitalized,&quot; &quot;well-managed&quot; and has at least a &quot;satisfactory&quot; rating under the CRA. &nbsp;In the first quarter of 2004, we elected to be treated as a financial holding company under the GLBA. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The GLBA establishes a system of functional regulation, under which the Federal Reserve Board will regulate the banking activities of financial holding companies and other federal regulators will regulate banks' financial subsidiaries. &nbsp;The Securities and Exchange Commission (the &#147;Commission&#148;) will regulate securities activities of financial holding companies and state insurance regulators will regulate their business activities. &nbsp;The GLBA also provides new protections against the transfer and use by financial institutions of consumers' non-public, personal information. </P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The GLBA also modifies other current financial laws, including laws related to financial privacy and community reinvestment. &nbsp;The new financial privacy provisions generally prohibit financial institutions, including TransCommunity, from disclosing nonpublic personal financial information to nonaffiliated third persons unless customers have the opportunity to &#147;opt out&#148; of the disclosure. </P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><I>Consumer Laws and Regulations. &nbsp;</I>The Banks are also subject to certain consumer laws and regulations that are designed to protect consumers in transactions with banks. &nbsp;While the list set forth herein is not exhaustive, these laws and regulations include the Truth in Lending Act, the Truth in Savings Act, the Electronic Funds Transfer Act, the Expedited Funds Availability Act, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the Fair Housing Act and the GLBA, among others. These laws and regulations mandate certain disclosure requirements and regulate the manner in which financial institutions must deal with customers when taking deposits, making loans to or engaging in other types of transactions with such customers. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><I>Economic and Monetary Policies.</I><B> &nbsp;</B>The operations of TransCommunity are affected not only by general economic conditions, but also by the economic and monetary policies of various regulatory authorities. In particular, the Federal Reserve regulates money, credit and interest rates in order to influence general economic conditions. These policies have a significant influence on overall growth and distribution of loans, investments and deposits and affect interest rates charged on loans or paid for time and savings deposits. Federal Reserve monetary policies have had a significant effect on the operating results of commercial banks in the past and are expected to continue to do so in the future. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
