<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px" align=justify><B>Item 1A.</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:60px" align=justify><B>Risk Factors</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>Bank of Powhatan and Bank of Goochland did experience, and Bank of Louisa and Bank of Rockbridge have experienced and continue to experience, significant start-up operating losses. &nbsp;We expect that any other de novo banks we establish will likely experience similar start-up operating losses.</I></B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The future success of our operations must be considered in light of the expenses, complications and delays frequently encountered in connection with the establishment of new banks and related financial services. &nbsp;Typically, new banks are not profitable in their first several years of operation. &nbsp;For instance, Bank of Powhatan reached operating profitability in 24 months and Bank of Goochland reached operating profitability in 20 months.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Bank of Louisa, which opened in April 2004, incurred net losses of $384 thousand during 2005. &nbsp;The Bank of Louisa reached profitability in 2006 with net income totaling $110 thousand for the year ending December 31, 2006. We expect that other new banks we may establish, such as the Bank of Rockbridge, will also experience start-up operating losses for an initial period.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>We have a limited operating history upon which to base any estimate of our future success.</I></B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>We were organized in 2001, and we and our subsidiaries have limited operating histories. &nbsp;As a consequence, there is limited historical financial information on which to base an evaluation of our current business or to make any estimate of our future performance. &nbsp;Because of our limited operating history, you may not have access to the type and amount of information that would be available to a shareholder of a financial institution with a more extended operating history.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>Many of the loans in our loan portfolio are not seasoned which may increase the risk of credit defaults in the future.</I></B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>A significant portion of Bank of Powhatan&#146;s loans have been originated in the past five years. &nbsp;All of Bank of Goochland&#146;s loans have been originated since November 2002, and most of Bank of Louisa&#146;s loans have been originated since April 2004. &nbsp;In general, loans do not begin to show signs of credit deterioration or default until they have been outstanding for some period of time, a process referred to as &#147;seasoning.&#148; &nbsp;As a result, a portfolio of older loans will usually behave more predictably than a newer portfolio. &nbsp;Because our loan portfolio is relatively new, the current level of delinquencies and defaults may not be representative of the level that will prevail when the portfolio becomes more seasoned, which may be higher than current levels. &nbsp;If delinquencies and defaults increase, we may be required to increase our provision for loan losses, which would adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>Our concentrations of loans may create a greater risk of loan defaults and losses.</I></B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>We have a substantial amount of loans secured by real estate in the central Virginia area, and substantially all of our loans are to borrowers in that area. &nbsp;Additionally, at December 31, 2006, approximately 74.8% of our loan portfolio consisted of commercial and residential construction loans, commercial real estate loans, commercial business loans and commercial lines of credit. &nbsp;These types of loans have a higher risk of default than other types of loans, such as single family residential mortgage loans. &nbsp;In addition, the repayments of these loans, which generally have larger balances than single family mortgage loans, often depend on the successful operation of a business or the sale or development of the underlying property, and as a result are more likely to be adversely affected by deteriorating conditions in the real estate market or the economy in general. &nbsp;These concentrations expose us to the risk that adverse developments in the real estate market, or in general economic conditions in the central Virginia/Richmond metropolitan area, could increase the levels of nonperforming loans and charge-offs, and reduce loan demand. &nbsp;In that event, we would likely experience additional losses. &nbsp;Additionally, if, for any reason, economic conditions in the area deteriorate, or there is significant volatility or weakness in the economy or any significant sector of the area&#146;s economy, our ability to develop our business relationships may be diminished, the quality and collectibility of our loans may be adversely affected, the value of collateral may decline and loan demand may be reduced. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>If our allowance for loan losses becomes inadequate, our results of operations may be adversely affected.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>We maintain an allowance for loan losses that we believe is adequate to absorb the estimated losses in our loan portfolio. &nbsp;Through periodic review of the loan portfolio, management determines the amount of the allowance for loan losses by considering, among other factors, general market conditions, credit quality of the loan portfolio and performance of our customers relative to their financial obligations with us. &nbsp;The amount of future losses is susceptible to changes in economic, operating and other conditions, including changes in interest rates that may be beyond our control, and these future losses may exceed our current estimates. &nbsp;There is no precise method for predicting credit losses since any estimate of loan losses is necessarily subjective and the accuracy depends on the outcome of future events. &nbsp;As a result, charge-offs in future periods may exceed our allowance for loan losses and additional increases in the allowance for loan losses would be required. &nbsp;If we need to make significant and unanticipated increases in our loan loss allowance in the future, our results of operations and financial condition would be materially adversely affected at that time.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>The markets for our services are highly competitive and we face substantial competition.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The banking business is highly competitive. &nbsp;We compete with other commercial banks, savings and loan associations, credit unions, finance companies, mutual funds, insurance companies and brokerage and investment banking firms soliciting business from residents of and businesses located in our markets. &nbsp;Many of our competitors enjoy competitive advantages, including greater financial resources, a wider geographic presence or more accessible branch office locations, the ability to offer additional services, more favorable pricing alternatives and lower origination and operating costs. &nbsp;Failure to compete effectively to attract new and to retain existing customers could result in a decrease in loans we originate and could negatively affect our results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>10</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>In attracting deposits, we compete with insured depository institutions such as banks, savings institutions and credit unions, as well as institutions offering uninsured investment alternatives, including money market funds. &nbsp;Traditional banking institutions, as well as entities intending to transact business online, are increasingly using the Internet to attract deposits without geographic or physical limitations. &nbsp;In addition, many non-bank competitors are not subject to the same extensive regulations that govern us. &nbsp;These competitors may offer higher interest rates on deposits than we offer, which could result in either our attracting fewer deposits or increasing our interest rates in order to attract deposits. &nbsp;Increased deposit competition could raise our cost of funds and could adversely affect our ability to generate the funds necessary for our lending operations, which would negatively affect our results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>Changes in interest rates could have an adverse effect on our income.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Our profitability depends to a large extent upon our net interest income. &nbsp;Net interest income is the difference between interest income on interest-earning assets, such as loans and investments, and interest expense on interest-bearing liabilities, such as deposits and borrowings. &nbsp;Our net interest income will be adversely affected if market interest rates change so that the interest we pay on deposits and borrowings increases faster than the interest we earn on loans and investments. &nbsp;Changes in interest rates also affect the value of our loans. &nbsp;An increase in interest rates could adversely affect borrowers&#146; ability to pay the principal or interest on existing loans or reduce their ability to borrow more money. &nbsp;This may lead to an increase in our nonperforming assets or a decrease in loan originations, either of which could have a material and negative effect on our results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Interest rates are highly sensitive to many factors that are partly or completely outside of our control, including governmental monetary policies, domestic and international economic and political conditions and general economic conditions such as inflation, recession, unemployment and money supply. &nbsp;Fluctuations in market interest rates are neither predictable nor controllable and may have a material and negative effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>We are subject to significant government regulations that affect our operations and may result in higher operating costs or increased competition for us.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Our success will depend not only on competitive factors, but also on state and federal regulations affecting financial and bank holding companies generally. &nbsp;We are subject to extensive regulation by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the Office of Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and to a lesser extent, the Virginia State Corporation Commission. &nbsp;Supervision, regulation and examination of banks and bank holding companies by bank regulatory agencies are intended primarily for the protection of depositors rather than shareholders. &nbsp;These agencies examine financial and bank holding companies and commercial banks, establish capital and other financial requirements and approve new branches, acquisitions or other changes of control. &nbsp;Our ability to establish new banks or branches or make acquisitions is conditioned on receiving required regulatory approvals from the applicable regulators.</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Regulations now affecting us may change at any time, and these changes could affect us in unpredictable and adverse ways. &nbsp;Such changes could subject us to additional costs, limit the types of financial services and products we may offer, increase the ability of non-banks to offer competing financial services and products, and/or assist competitors that are not subject to similar regulation, among other things. &nbsp;Failure to comply with laws, regulations or policies could result in sanctions by regulatory agencies, civil money penalties and damage to our reputation, which could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operation. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>Our success will depend significantly upon general economic conditions in central Virginia and nationally.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Our success will depend significantly upon general economic conditions in central Virginia as well as national economic conditions affecting Virginia. &nbsp;Any prolonged economic downturn or recession affecting central Virginia could impair borrowers&#146; ability to repay existing loans, potentially causing an increase in our nonperforming assets and charge-offs; deter customers from incurring more debt, possibly decreasing loan originations; or cause customers to draw down their savings, potentially decreasing deposits. &nbsp;In that event, we may experience lower earnings or losses, impaired liquidity and the erosion of capital. &nbsp;Such an economic downturn or recession could result from a variety of causes, including natural disasters, a prolonged downturn in various industries upon which the economy of central Virginia depends, or a national recession.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>In addition, one of the focal points of our business is serving the banking and financial services needs of small to medium-sized businesses. &nbsp;These businesses generally have fewer financial resources in terms of capital or borrowing capacity relative to larger entities. &nbsp;As such, the businesses of many of our customers and their ability to repay outstanding loans may be more sensitive to changes in general economic conditions than larger entities. &nbsp;As a consequence, our results of operations and financial condition could be adversely affected by weakening economic conditions in central Virginia and nationally.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>We depend on the services of key personnel, and a loss of any of those personnel could disrupt our operations and could have a material adverse effect on our operations.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>We are a customer-focused and relationship-driven organization. &nbsp;Our growth and success has been in large part driven by the personal customer relationships maintained by our executives. &nbsp;We depend on the performance of our management at the holding company as well as the presidents of each of our subsidiary banks. &nbsp;Although we have entered into employment agreements with certain of our executive officers, we cannot offer any assurance that they and other key employees will remain employed by us. &nbsp;Moreover, we do not maintain key man life insurance on any of our executive officers. &nbsp;The loss of services of one or more of these key employees could have a material adverse impact on our operations. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B><I>Failure to maintain effective systems of internal and disclosure control could have a material adverse effect on our results of operation and financial condition. &nbsp;</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>11</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Effective internal and disclosure controls are necessary for us to provide reliable financial reports and effectively prevent fraud and to operate successfully as a public company. &nbsp;If we cannot provide reliable financial reports or prevent fraud, our reputation and operating results would be harmed. &nbsp;As part of our ongoing monitoring of internal control we may discover material weaknesses or significant deficiencies in our internal control as defined under standards adopted by the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, or PCAOB, that require remediation. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Subsequent to the filing of the original Form 10-KSB for the year ended December 31, 2005, we determined that there was a material weakness in our internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2005 arising from our methods of accounting and documentation for loans participated to third parties. &nbsp;Under the PCAOB standards, a &#147;material weakness&#148; is a control deficiency, or combination of control deficiencies, that results in more than a remote likelihood that a material misstatement of the annual or interim financial statements will not be prevented or detected. &nbsp;We also identified a significant deficiency in internal control over financial reporting arising from our methods of accounting and record generation and maintenance for loan origination costs and for amortizing fees. &nbsp;We have provided additional information on this material weakness and this significant deficiency, including our remediation of them, in Item 9A, &#147;Controls and Procedures,&#148; below. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>We cannot assure that other internal or disclosure control deficiencies might not be identified. &nbsp;Any failure to maintain effective controls or timely effect any necessary improvement of our internal and disclosure controls could, among other things, result in losses from fraud or error, harm our reputation or cause investors to lose confidence in our reported financial information, all of which could have a material adverse effect on our results of operation and financial condition. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>The success of our future recruiting efforts will impact our ability to grow.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The implementation of our business strategy will require us to continue to attract, hire, motivate and retain skilled personnel to develop new customer relationships as well as new financial products and services. &nbsp;Many experienced banking professionals employed by our competitors are covered by agreements not to compete or solicit their existing customers if they were to leave their current employment. &nbsp;These agreements make the recruitment of these professionals more difficult. The market for these people is competitive, and we cannot assure you that we will be successful in attracting, hiring, motivating or retaining them. &nbsp;The success of our recruiting efforts may impact our ability to grow and our future profitability.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><B><I>We will not be in a position to pay dividends for the foreseeable future.</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>&nbsp;We do not expect to pay dividends on our common stock for at least several years. &nbsp;We intend to retain future earnings, if any, to improve each subsidiary bank&#146;s capital structure to support future growth. &nbsp;Consequently, the return on our stock, if any, may be limited to capital appreciation for an indefinite period. &nbsp;Our future dividend policy will depend in large part on the earnings of our subsidiary banks, capital requirements, financial condition and other factors considered relevant by our Board of Directors. Additionally, TransCommunity is a separate legal entity from its subsidiaries and does not have significant operations or revenues of its own. &nbsp;TransCommunity substantially depends on dividends from its subsidiaries to pay its operating expenses. &nbsp;The availability of dividends from the subsidiaries is limited by various statutes and regulations. &nbsp;In the event that its subsidiaries are not permitted to pay dividends due to federal or state regulations, TransCommunity may not be able to pay its operating expenses. &nbsp;Consequently, any future inability to receive dividends from its subsidiaries could adversely affect TransCommunity&#146;s business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B><I>To implement our growth strategy, we must successfully identify opportunities for expansion and successfully integrate our new operations into our existing operating platform. &nbsp;&nbsp;</I></B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>We intend to continue our current growth strategy of entering underserved or over-consolidated markets in Virginia by organizing <I>de novo</I> banks, opportunistically acquiring other banking institutions or establishing branches of our existing subsidiaries. &nbsp;To the extent we are unable to identify attractive markets to enter, an important component of our growth strategy may be lost. &nbsp;Additionally, any future expansion or acquisition efforts may entail substantial costs and may not produce the revenue, earnings or synergies that we had anticipated. &nbsp;Any future expansion or acquisitions that we undertake will involve operational risks and uncertainties. &nbsp;Acquired companies may have unforeseen liabilities, exposure to asset quality problems, key employee and customer retention problems and other problems that could negatively affect our organization. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>We may not be able to successfully integrate the operations, management, products and services of the entities that we acquire or establish with our existing Common Operating Platform. &nbsp;The integration process may also require significant time and attention from our management that they would otherwise direct at servicing existing business and developing new business. Our failure to successfully integrate any entities that we establish or acquire into our existing operations may increase our operating costs significantly and adversely affect our business and earnings.</P>
<P style="line-height:16.667px; margin-top:20px; margin-bottom:-16.667px" align=justify><B>Item 1B.</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:60px" align=justify><B>Unresolved Staff Comments</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>None.</P>
<P style="line-height:16.667px; margin-top:20px; margin-bottom:-16.667px" align=justify><B>Item 2.</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:60px" align=justify><B>Properties</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-right:-2.867px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>TransCommunity&#146;s headquarters are located in approximately 14,000 square feet of leased space at 4235 Innslake Drive, Glen Allen, Virginia. This office space was leased in September 2003 and occupied in December, 2003. The office houses corporate operations, along with executive officers. &nbsp;The lease is for 10 years.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-right:-2.867px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Bank of Powhatan is located at 2320 Anderson Highway, Powhatan, Virginia. &nbsp;This bank&#146;s building, which is of new construction, is a two-story brick structure, containing approximately 6,000 square feet. &nbsp;It has four teller stations, three drive-through windows and a drive-up ATM and night depository. &nbsp;The bank owns this property.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-right:-2.867px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Bank of Goochland is located at 100 Broad Street Road, Manakin-Sabot, Virginia. &nbsp;This bank&#146;s main office building, which is of new construction, is a two-story brick structure containing approximately 9,500 square feet. &nbsp;It has five teller stations, two drive-through windows and a drive-up ATM and a night depository. &nbsp;The bank owns this property.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>12</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>

<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-right:-2.867px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Bank of Goochland also operates a branch office in a leased facility located at Goochland Courthouse, containing approximately 1,400 square feet. &nbsp;The term of this lease is five years.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-right:-2.867px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Bank of Louisa is located at 217 East Main Street, in the Town of Louisa, Virginia. &nbsp;This bank&#146;s building, which is of new construction, is a two-story brick structure containing approximately 9,000 square feet. &nbsp;It has four teller stations, two drive-through windows, a drive-up ATM and a night depository facility. &nbsp;The bank owns this property.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-right:-2.867px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Bank of Rockbridge located at 744 North Lee Highway in the City of Lexington, Virginia. &nbsp;This bank&#146;s building, which was an existing bank building, is a two story brick structure containing approximately 4,200 square feet. &nbsp;It has three teller stations, a drive-through window, a walk-up ATM and a night depository facility. &nbsp;The bank leases the premises with an option after three years to extend the life of the lease for additional terms.</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company believes that all of its properties are adequately covered by insurance. &nbsp;In addition, all of the Company&#146;s properties are in good operating condition and are adequate for the Company&#146;s present and anticipated future needs.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>See Notes 7 and 20 of the notes to consolidated financial statements for more information on the Company&#146;s properties.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:15.6px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-15.6px" align=justify><B>Item 3.</B></P>
<P style="line-height:12.933px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:60px" align=justify><B>Legal Proceedings</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-right:-2.867px; text-indent:48px">In the ordinary course of operations, TransCommunity and subsidiaries expect to be parties to various legal proceedings. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>On June 14, 2006, an individual and a company controlled by the individual (Dean H. Gould and Cal-Flo Investments, LLC) filed a lawsuit against Main Street Mortgage &amp; Investment Corporation (&#147;Main Street&#148;), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bank of Powhatan, and five other defendants that are not affiliated with Main Street in the General Court of Justice, Superior Court Division, in Wake County, North Carolina. &nbsp;The lawsuit arises from three properties on which Main Street originated mortgage loans. &nbsp;The loans at issue were made by third-party lenders, and neither the Company nor any of its subsidiary banks hold any of the loans for its own account. &nbsp;The plaintiffs allege that the defendants developed a fraudulent scheme to originate these mortgage loans through Main Street employing, with Main Street&#146;s knowledge, inflated appraisals and other devices that resulted in damages to the plaintiffs in the aggregate amount of $100,000 to $150,000. &nbsp;The plaintiffs have requested both compensatory and punitive damages.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Main Street filed an answer to the lawsuit and denies any liability. &nbsp;There has been no further activity in the lawsuit from any other party, and Main Street has ceased its business operations and filed for dissolution under applicable Virginia law.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At the present time, the case is in the early stages, there has been no discovery, and accordingly, the Company can not conclude on the outcome or estimate any potential loss.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-right:-2.4px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>On November 2, 2006, James L. Minter filed a lawsuit against the Company and William C. Wiley, the former Chief Executive Officer and Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Company, in the Circuit Court of the County of Powhatan in Virginia. &nbsp;The suit arises out of the purchase of Main Street Mortgage and Investment Corporation by Bank of Powhatan in early 2001. &nbsp;Mr. Minter alleges that in late 2000 Wiley withheld information concerning the value of Main Street Mortgage from the Bank&#146;s Board of Directors and that the Bank would not have acquired Main Street Mortgage if the valuation had been provided to the Bank&#146;s board. &nbsp;Mr. Minter&#146;s suit claims that the Company aided and abetted and conspired with Wiley in his misrepresentation of Main Street Mortgage&#146;s value. &nbsp;Mr. Minter&#146;s suit also alleges that the December 2005 separation agreement between the Company and William Wiley improperly released claims the Company had against Wiley arising out of Wiley&#146;s alleged concealment of the Main Street Mortgage valuation from the Bank&#146;s board in late 2000. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Minter seeks unspecified recessionary and compensatory damages, unspecified treble damages and punitive damages of $350,000 against each defendant, jointly and severally and with interest. &nbsp;Minter also seeks to recover his attorneys&#146; fees. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company believes that insofar as it concerns the Company, Mr. Minter&#146;s suit is without merit.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company has moved for a dismissal; has brought claims against Mr. Minter for breach of fiduciary duty related to his use of confidential Company information for personal gain; and has removed him from the board of the Bank.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Based on the facts presently known, the Company believes it has limited liability exposure arising from this lawsuit. &nbsp;However, since the case is in the very early stages, the Company is unable to evaluate the likelihood of an unfavorable outcome or to estimate the amount or range of potential loss, if any, in this matter. &nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>

<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-right:-2.867px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>During the quarter ended December 31, 2006, no matters were submitted for a vote of security holders.</P>

<P style="line-height:13.333px; margin:0px"><B>Dividend Policy</B></P>
<P style="line-height:13.333px; margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>TransCommunity has not declared or distributed any cash dividends to its shareholders, and it is not likely that any cash dividends will be declared for several years. &nbsp;The Board of Directors of TransCommunity intends to follow a policy of retaining any earnings to provide funds to operate and expand the business of TransCommunity and its subsidiaries for the foreseeable future. &nbsp;The future dividend policy of TransCommunity is subject to the discretion of the Board of Directors and will depend upon a number of factors, including future earnings, financial condition, cash requirements and general business conditions. &nbsp;TransCommunity&#146;s ability to distribute cash dividends will depend substantially upon the ability of its subsidiaries to pay dividends to TransCommunity. &nbsp;TransCommunity&#146;s banks are subject to legal limitations on the amount of dividends each is permitted to pay. &nbsp;Furthermore, neither the banks nor TransCommunity may declare or pay a cash dividend on their capital stock if they are insolvent or if the payment of the dividend would render them insolvent or unable to pay their obligations as they become due in the ordinary course of business. &nbsp;See &#147;Limits on Dividends and Other Payments&#148; in Part I of this annual report.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><B>Critical Accounting Policies</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Certain critical accounting policies reflect significant judgments and estimates used in the preparation of our consolidated financial statements. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s most critical accounting policy relates to our allowance for loan losses, which reflects the estimated losses resulting from the inability of our borrowers to make required payments. &nbsp;If the financial condition of our borrowers were to deteriorate, resulting in an impairment of their ability to make payments, our estimates would be updated, and additional allowances might be required. &nbsp;For further discussion of the estimates used in determining the allowance for loan losses, we refer you to the discussion on &#147;Provision for Loan Losses&#148; below.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Overview</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>During 2006, TransCommunity reported its first net profit of $117 thousand, versus a loss for the year 2005 of $1.8 million. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s 2006 results thus represent a year-over-year improvement of $1.9 million. Over the same period, income per share, both basic and diluted, improved from a loss of $0.53 to a profit of $0.03.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Net income from continuing operations totaled $919 thousand for the year ended 2006 as compared to a loss of $1.3 million for the year ended 2005, an improvement of $2.3 million. Over the same period earnings per share from continuing operations improved $0.61 per share from a loss of $0.41 in 2005 to a gain of $0.20 during 2006. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Operating results for 2006 were impacted by two significant events. First, during the third quarter of 2006, TransCommunity Financial Corporation (the &#147;Company&#148;) determined that it had incorrectly accounted for loans subject to certain loan participation agreements entered into with third-party financial institutions. Under the direction of the audit committee of its Board of Directors, the Company completed an evaluation of the manner in which it accounted for loan participation agreements. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>As a result, the Company filed an amendment to its annual report on Form 10-KSB for the year ended December 31, 2005. &nbsp;As a result of the restatement, the Company&#146;s period end total loans and secured borrowings were increased by $12.5 million and $7.2 million at December 31, 2005 and 2004, respectively. In addition, interest income on loans and interest expense on other borrowings were also increased by $550 thousand and $112 thousand for the years ended December 31, 2005 and 2004 respectively. None of the adjustments resulting from the restatement had any impact on the company&#146;s net worth at any date or on its net income, net interest income, noninterest income or noninterest expense for any period. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Second, on November 29, 2006, the Board of Directors of TransCommunity directed management to close Main Street Mortgage &amp; Investment Corporation (&#147;Main Street&#148;), a mortgage brokerage company. Main Street had operated as a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Bank of Powhatan, a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Company, since 2001. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, TransCommunity had on a consolidated basis, total assets of $198.4 million, total deposits of $165.0 million, total loans of $151.4 million and total stockholders&#146; equity of $30.6 million. In comparison at December 31, 2005 and 2004 TransCommunity reported total assets of $190.6 million and $150.3 million, total deposits of $146.6 million and $123.7 million, total loans of $135.1 million and $112.1 million and total stockholders&#146; equity of $30.4 million and $14.9 million respectively.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>On February 7, 2007, the Company announced the consolidation of the charters of its four bank subsidiaries into a single legal entity. The consolidation of the bank charters will provide significant financial advantages for our shareholders, as the costs associated with operating under multiple charters are reduced or eliminated.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>During 2006, the Company continued to experience changes in its management team and Board of Directors. &nbsp;During the first quarter of 2006, Messrs Agee, Crowder, Metts, Minter and J. Purcell submitted their resignations as directors of the Company. &nbsp;Acting on the recommendation of the Company&#146;s Nominating &amp; Governance Committee, the Board, appointed a total of six new directors during 2006, including Messrs. Bozard, Broomall, Claeys, Miller, D. Purcell and Zoeller. &nbsp;In the fourth quarter of 2006, and in January, 2007, Messrs Broomall, Claeys, Nuckols and D. Purcell submitted their resignations as directors of the Company. &nbsp;Additionally, in January, 2007, the Company&#146;s Chief Financial Officer, Mr. Littreal, submitted his resignation as an officer of the Company in order to take a similar position at a larger organization.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Discontinued operations</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>In 2006, management continued to implement cost control measures in its operating units. In November of 2006, the Board approved the closing of Main Street Mortgage and Investment Corporation. &nbsp;These measures enable the Company to better align its operations with its community banking focus. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>18</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Main Street was acquired by the Bank of Powhatan in 2001,<FONT COLOR=#FF0000> </FONT>had generated revenues of $1.9 million and $3.9 million in the years 2006 and 2005. Expenses during the same periods were $2.7 million and $4.0 million. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>During 2005, Main Street originated residential and commercial mortgage loans of $162 million, generated gross revenues of $3.9 million, and incurred net losses of $84 thousand. &nbsp;In 2006, The operations of Main Street resulted in a net loss from discontinued operations of $802 thousand in 2006. Management completed the dissolution of Main Street in the 1<SUP>st</SUP> quarter of 2007.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>During 2004, we established a financial services division to enable our subsidiary banks to offer trust banking, asset management and insurance and securities brokerage services to our customers. &nbsp;To support these activities, we sought and received regulatory approval to exercise trust banking powers through each of our subsidiary banks. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>During 2005, losses from financial service activities totaled $339 thousand. &nbsp;As a result, during the fourth quarter of 2005, the TransCommunity Board of Directors voted to discontinue offering these services in-house and directed management to establish more cost-effective ways to deliver investment products. &nbsp;In the first quarter of 2006, our Financial Services operations were integrated into our community banking business segment. &nbsp;See <A NAME="OLE_LINK1"></A><A NAME="OLE_LINK2"></A>&#147;Management&#146;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operation &#150; Financial Services&#148; in Item 7 of this annual report.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Community Banking Segment </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px">&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Net income for the community banking segment was $2.4 million, an increase of $703 thousand over 2005 net income of $1.7 million. Net interest income grew by $1.6 million, or 22.1%, as a result of increased loan volumes and higher yields. &nbsp;Deposit interest expense benefited from relatively low interest rates as a $17.1 million increase in average deposit balances resulted in only a $1.6 million increase in interest expense on deposits. The provision for loan losses increased $227 thousand largely as a result the growth in our loan portfolio of $16.3 million. &nbsp;Noninterest income in the community banking segment increased by $297 thousand to $975 thousand during 2006. &nbsp;Noninterest expense in the community banking segment increased by $265 thousand, or 4.5%, while assets grew by $19.1 million, or 10.7%. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Mortgage Segment </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Main Street&#146;s total revenue in 2006 totaled $1.9 million verses $3.9 million in 2005, a 51.3% decrease. &nbsp;Losses amounted to $802 thousand compared to $84 thousand in 2005. Confronted with increasing losses, as well as the difficulty of turning around this non-core business, the Board of Directors on November 29, 2006 approved the closing of Main Street. Main Street had operated as a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bank of Powhatan, which is a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Company, since 2001. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Financial Services Segment </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-right:-2.4px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>Due to continued losses in this segment, the Board of Directors voted in the fourth quarter of 2005 to cease operations. The trust department at each of the banks was effectively discontinued at December 31, 2005 and management reorganized the remaining financial services during the quarter ending March 2006 and integrated the remaining Financial Services operations into the community banking segment. For the year ending 2005, the Company realized a loss of $339 thousand from this discontinued operation. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-right:-2.4px" align=justify><B>Financial Condition at December 31, 2006</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-right:-2.4px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>During the year ended December 31, 2006, our assets increased by $7.8 million, or 4.1%, to 198.4 million. Of this increase in total assets, $8.8 million represented growth in interest-earning assets, while non-interest bearing assets declined by $1.0 million. Continued strong loan demand throughout the year resulted in an increase of $16.3 million, or 12.1%, in total loans outstanding. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-right:-2.4px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>During 2006, investment securities increased by $3.8 million to $35.0 million. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-right:-2.4px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>Loan growth in 2006 was concentrated in the commercial and industrial and real estate lending portfolios. Our total loan growth of $16.3 million in 2006 was the result of an $11.1 million or 54.8 % increase in commercial and industrial loans from $20.2 million to $31.3 million, and a $4.3 million or 4.0% increase from $106.6 million to $110.9 million in real estate loans.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-right:-2.4px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>Customer deposits continue to be our primary funding source. Our deposits are primarily generated through our community banks. At December 31, 2006, deposits totaled $165.0 million, an increase of $18.4 million or 12.5 % from year-end 2005. Time deposits increased $23.5 million. This increase of $23.5 million was offset by a reduction of $8.3 million in interest bearing demand deposits and $12.5 million in securitized borrowings during 2006. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-right:-2.4px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>Our capital position remains strong, with all of our regulatory capital ratios at levels that categorize us as &#147;well capitalized&#148; under bank regulatory capital guidelines. At December 31, 2006, our shareholder equity totaled $30.6 million, an increase of $200 thousand from the December 31, 2005 balance. &nbsp;This increase in shareholder equity is primarily the result of the Company achieving a net profit for 2006. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:5.533px; margin-bottom:5.533px"><B>Net Interest Income</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:5.533px; margin-bottom:5.533px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Like most financial institutions, the primary component of our earnings is net interest income. Net interest income is the difference between interest income, principally from loans and investments, and interest expense, principally on customer deposits and borrowings. Changes in net interest income result from changes in volume and changes in interest rates earned and paid. By volume, we mean the average dollar level of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities. Spread refers to the difference between the average yield on interest-earning assets and the average cost of interest-bearing liabilities, and margin refers to net interest income divided by average interest-earning assets. Spread and margin are influenced by the levels and relative mix of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities, as well as by levels of noninterest-bearing liabilities. During the years ended December&nbsp;31, 2006 and 2005, our average interest-earning assets were $181.1&nbsp;million, and $158.5&nbsp;million, respectively. During these same years, our net interest margins were 5.14% and 4.68%, respectively. </P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:96px"><BR>
<B><I>Average Balances and Average Rates Earned and Paid. </I></B>The table contained in Schedule I on page 33 sets forth, for the years 2006, 2005 and 2004, information with regard to average balances of assets and liabilities, as well as the total dollar amounts of interest income from interest-earning assets and interest expense on interest-bearing liabilities, resultant yields or costs, net interest income, net interest spread, net interest margin and ratio of average interest-earning assets to average interest-bearing liabilities. Average loans include nonaccruing loans, the effect of which is to lower the average yield.<A NAME="FIS_UNIDENTIFIED_TABLE_8"></A></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><B>Results of Operations </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Net Income</I>. </B>&nbsp;Our net income for 2006 was $117 thousand, an improvement of $1.9 million and $2.7 million from net losses of $1.8&nbsp;million and $2.6 million in 2005 and 2004, respectively. &nbsp;Net income per share, both basic and diluted, was $0.03 for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2006, reflecting per share increases of $0.56 and $1.25 when compared to per share losses of $0.53 and $1.22 per share for the years ended December 31, 2005 and 2004, respectively. &nbsp;Total assets averaged $192.1&nbsp;million during 2006 as compared to $170.3&nbsp;million in 2005, an increase of $21.8 million or 12.8%. &nbsp;Total average assets increased $67.4 million or 54.1% when comparing 2006 to 2004.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>During 2006, the prime rate increased 100 basis points, and we have benefited from our asset sensitive balance sheet position. &nbsp;While it is management&#146;s goal to remain relatively interest rate neutral, our Company is currently asset sensitive and does benefit from a rising interest rate environment. &nbsp;As a result of our continued growth in interest-earning assets during 2006, combined with slower growth in funding costs and rising interest rates, our net interest income increased $1.9&nbsp;million, or 25.3% from the year ended December 31, 2005 to the year ended December 31, 2006.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:49.533px" align=justify>During 2005, we continued to experience strong growth at each of our subsidiary banks and we were able to raise sufficient capital to support our growth strategy. &nbsp;Total assets averaged $170.3&nbsp;million during 2005 as compared to $124.6&nbsp;million in 2004, an increase of $45.7 million or 36.7%. &nbsp;During 2005, the prime rate increased 200 basis points. &nbsp;As a result of our growth in interest-earning assets during 2005, combined with low funding costs and rising interest rates, our net interest income increased $2.5&nbsp;million, or 52.1% during that year. &nbsp;The growth in our non-interest expense during 2005 included some non-recurring restructuring related costs, which totaled $302 thousand or $0.09 per share. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:49.533px" align=justify>In absolute terms, our net interest income after the provision for loan losses increased by $1.7&nbsp;million or 23.1%, when comparing 2006 to 2005, while our non-interest income grew by $220 thousand and our non-interest expense decreased by $401 thousand. &nbsp;When comparing 2005 to 2004, our net interest income after the provision for loan losses increased by $2.8&nbsp;million, while our non-interest income grew by $29 thousand from continuing operations. &nbsp;However, this income growth was largely offset by the increase in non-interest expenses from continuing operations of $1.9 million arising from increased salaries and benefits. &nbsp;Additional details on these components of net income are described below.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Net Interest Income</I>. </B>&nbsp;Our net interest income increased to $9.3 million for the year ended December 31, 2006, an increase of $1.9&nbsp;million, or 25.3%, over net interest income for 2005. &nbsp;Our growth in interest income was the result of growth in our level of average earning assets as well as continued strong loan demand. &nbsp;Average total interest-earning assets increased $22.6&nbsp;million or 14.3%, during 2006 as compared to 2005, while our average yield increased by 101 basis points from 6.88% during 2005 to 7.89% during 2006. &nbsp;The interest rates earned on a significant portion of our loans adjust immediately when index rates such as our prime rate changes. &nbsp;Conversely, most of our interest-bearing liabilities, including certificates of deposit and borrowings, have rates fixed until maturity. &nbsp;As a result, interest rate increases generally result in an immediate increase in our interest income on loans. &nbsp;There is a delayed impact on interest expense because 64.4% of our average interest-bearing deposits were classified as time deposits, which only experience increases in interest costs upon renewal. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Our average total interest-bearing liabilities increased by $11.4 million, or 8.9%, from 2005 to 2006. &nbsp;With rates consistently increasing during 2006, our average cost of interest-bearing liabilities increased by 84 basis points from 2.73% during 2005 to 3.57% during 2006, allowing our interest rate spread to increase by 17 basis points. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:49.533px" align=justify>Our average total interest-bearing liabilities increased by $35.1 million, or 37.7%, from 2004 to 2005. &nbsp;With rates consistently increasing during 2005, our average cost of interest-bearing liabilities increased by 59 basis points from 2.14% during 2004 to 2.73% during 2005, allowing our interest rate spread to increase 33 basis points. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:49.533px" align=justify>During 2005, our net interest income increased by $2.5&nbsp;million, or 52.1%, to $7.4&nbsp;million, when compared to 2004. &nbsp;Our growth in interest income for 2005 was the result of growth in our level of average earning assets as well as continued strong loan demand. &nbsp;Average total interest-earning assets increased $43.2&nbsp;million or 37.5%, during 2005 as compared to 2004, while our average yield increased by 92 basis points from 5.96% during 2004 to 6.88% in 2005. &nbsp;For 2005, 58.9% of our average interest-bearing deposits were classified as time deposits. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:49.533px" align=justify>&nbsp;Our investment income and interest expense for 2005 was impacted by the July 2005 stock offering in which TransCommunity completed the sale of 2.3 million shares of its common stock. &nbsp;&nbsp;A portion of the net proceeds from this offering was used to repay the outstanding principal balance of $1.45 million and accrued interest on TransCommunity&#146;s operating line of credit. &nbsp;&nbsp;TransCommunity used $3.3 million of the proceeds from this offering to strengthen the capital position of two of its subsidiary banks, which improved their respective lending limits.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2006, our net interest spread was 4.32%; our net interest margin was 5.14%. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2005, our net interest spread was 4.15%; our net interest margin was 4.68%. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2004, our net interest spread was 3.82%; our net interest margin was 4.23%. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Provision for Loan Losses. </I></B>We recorded a $493&nbsp;thousand provision for loan losses for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2006, representing an increase of $227 thousand from the $266 thousand provision expense for 2005, but less than the $549 thousand recorded in 2004. &nbsp;The level of the loan loss provision for these years is consistent with loan growth and net charge-offs that we experienced. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Provisions for loan losses are charged to income to bring our allowance for loan losses at period end to a level deemed appropriate by management based on the factors discussed under &#147;Asset Quality - Allowance for Loan Losses.&#148; &nbsp;While the dollar amount of the provision for loan losses increased on a year-over-year basis, the ratio of the allowance for loan losses to period-ending total loans only increased 17 basis points from 1.19% to 1.36%. &nbsp;Nonperforming loans totaled $961&nbsp;thousand or 0.6% of total loans at December&nbsp;31, 2006. &nbsp;Nonperforming loans totaled $165&nbsp;thousand or 0.12% of total loans at December&nbsp;31, 2005. &nbsp;The Company reported no nonperforming loans at December&nbsp;31, 2004.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>22</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The allowance for loan losses at December&nbsp;31, 2006 of $2.1&nbsp;million represents 1.36% of total loans and 214.9% of nonperforming loans. &nbsp;The allowance for loan losses at December&nbsp;31, 2005 of $1.6&nbsp;million equaled 1.19% of total loans outstanding at that date. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Non-Interest Income</I>. &nbsp;</B>For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2006, non-interest income from continuing operations increased $220 thousand, or 27.7%, to $1.0&nbsp;million from $800 thousand for the prior year. &nbsp;The increase in non-interest income resulted primarily from an increase in service charges and fees on deposit accounts.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:49.533px" align=justify>For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2005, non-interest income from continuing operations increased slightly over the amount for 2004. &nbsp;Service charges and fees on deposit accounts increased by 3.8%, to $791 thousand during 2005. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Non-Interest Expense</I>. </B>We strive to maintain non-interest expenses at levels that we believe are appropriate given the nature of our operations and the need to invest in personnel and facilities to support our growth. &nbsp;Our ratio of non-interest expenses from continuing operations to average total assets during 2006 declined to 4.65% as compared to 5.48% during 2005. &nbsp;We were better able to control non-interest expense during the year despite our continued growth. &nbsp;For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 2006, non-interest expense decreased $401 thousand, or 4.3%, over 2005. &nbsp;Salary and employee benefits expense decreased $407 thousand, or 8.0%, including (i) the non-recurring restructuring charges in 2005 and 2006, (ii) pre-opening expenses at the Bank of Rockbridge, (iii) merit adjustments to salaries and (iv) increased benefit costs. &nbsp;Net occupancy expense increased $75 thousand, or 12.2%, reflecting the expenses associated with our normal operations.</P>

<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify><B><I>Income Taxes.</I> </B>At December 31, 2006, TransCommunity had total net operating loss (&#147;NOL&#148;) carryforwards of $7.5 million, which begin to expire in 2021.&nbsp; For 2006, the Company utilized $1 million of the NOL carryforward to offset taxable income.&nbsp; Under the Alternative Minimum Tax (&quot;AMT&quot;) system, the utilization of an AMT NOL carryover is limited to 90% of the AMT taxable income.&nbsp; This limitation resulted in an AMT tax liability of $15 thousand, which has been recorded in this year's statement of operations.&nbsp; This AMT is available as a credit to reduce regular tax liability in future years,&nbsp; The AMT credit carryover is included in deferred tax assets, subject to the valuation allowance discussed below.&nbsp; Under Section 382 of the Internal Revenue Code, if a corporation undergoes an &#147;ownership change&#148; (generally defined as a greater than 50% change in its equity ownership over a three-year period), the corporation&#146;s ability to use its pre-ownership change net operating loss carryforwards and certain other pre-ownership change tax attributes against its post-ownership change income may be limited.&nbsp; The stock offerings consummated in July 2005, and in 2002 were &quot;ownership changes&quot; which triggered Section 382 and limits the annual utilization of pre-ownership change net operating losses in post-ownership change years.&nbsp; To the extent the NOL limitation amount in any taxable year exceeds our taxable income in that year, the excess can be carried over effectively to increase the limitation in the next succeeding year or years.&nbsp; Given that none of TransCommunity&#146;s NOLs begin to expire until 2021, TransCommunity believes it will be able to fully utilize its NOLs prior to their respective expiration dates.&nbsp; Management will continue to monitor the Company&#146;s trend toward profitable operations and when sufficient evidence of future taxable income becomes available, the Company will reduce the valuation allowance and recognize the related tax benefit in the statement of operations.&nbsp; See Note 12 of the notes to the Company&#146;s consolidated financial statements elsewhere in this annual report for information concerning our NOLs.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:49.533px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, and December 31, 2005, TransCommunity had NOL carryforwards of $7.5 million and $8.5 million, respectively. &nbsp;No provision for income tax benefits associated with these NOLs has been recorded in the statement of operations since there is insufficient evidence to conclude that TransCommunity would produce taxable income in the future. &nbsp;Accordingly, the deferred tax asset related to the tax loss carryforwards and other deferred tax assets have been fully reduced by a valuation allowance.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><B>Investment Portfolio</B></P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company currently manages its investment securities portfolio consistent with established policies that include guidelines for Investment quality, rate sensitivity, liquidity and pledging needs on a bank by bank basis. &nbsp;This investment function will be centralized under the proposed centralization of operations and charter collapsing process. The aggregate investment portfolio approximates 115% of the Company&#146;s consolidated shareholders&#146; equity.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company accounts for securities under FASB Statement No. 115, Accounting for Certain Investments in Debt and Equity Securities. &nbsp;This standard requires classification of investments into three categories, &#147;held to maturity&#148; (&#147;HTM&#148;), &#147;available for sale&#148; (&#147;AFS&#148;), or &#147;trading,&#148; as further defined in Note 1 to the Company&#146;s Consolidated Financial Statements. &nbsp;The Company does not maintain a trading account and has classified no securities in this category. &nbsp;HTM securities are required to be carried on the financial statements at amortized cost. &nbsp;AFS securities are carried on the financial statements at fair value. &nbsp;The unrealized gains or losses, net of deferred income taxes, are reflected in shareholders&#146; equity. &nbsp;The HTM classification places restrictions on the Company&#146;s ability to sell securities or to transfer securities into the AFS classification. &nbsp;At December 31, 2006, 61.2% of the portfolio was classified as HTM.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company holds in its loan and securities portfolios, investments that adjust or float according to changes in &#147;prime&#148; lending rate. &nbsp;These holdings are not considered speculative but instead necessary for good asset/liability management.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The carrying value of the securities portfolio was $35.0 million at December 31, 2006, an increase of $3.8 million or 11.9% from the carrying value of $31.2 million at December 31, 2005. &nbsp;The market value of the AFS securities at December 31, 2006 was $13.6 million. &nbsp;The unrealized loss on the AFS securities was $40 thousand at December 31, 2006. &nbsp;The reduction in the net market value loss at December 31, 2006 is reflective of the continued rise in market interest rates. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Since the Bank anticipates much of the balance sheet growth to be experienced during 2007, if any, to be in the form of net portfolio loans, specific strategies will be executed during the early part of 2007 to maintain the investment portfolio at an amount comparable to the December 31, 2006 balances. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><B>Concentration of Credit Risk</B></P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>TransCommunity has a concentration of loans to borrowers secured by commercial real estate. &nbsp;At December 31, 2006, loans to these borrowers amounted to $60.6 million, or 40.0% of our consolidated loan portfolio. This compares with $65.5 million and $48.7 million and 48.5 % and 43.4% for the years 2005 and 2004, respectively. </P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><B>&nbsp;Asset Quality &#150; Allowance for Loan Losses </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The allowance for loan losses represents management&#146;s estimate of the amount deemed adequate to provide for potential losses in the loan portfolio. Among other factors, management considers the Company&#146;s historical loss experience, the size and composition of the loan portfolio, the value and adequacy of collateral and guarantors, non-performing credits and current and anticipated economic conditions. There are additional risks of future loan losses, which cannot be precisely quantified nor attributed to particular loans or classes of loans. Because those risks include general economic trends as well as conditions affecting individual borrowers, the allowance for loan losses is an estimate. The allowance is also subject to regulatory examinations and determination as to adequacy, which may take into account such factors as the methodology used to calculate the allowance and size of the allowance in comparison to peer companies identified by regulatory agencies. </P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Management maintains a list of loans which have a potential weakness that may need special attention. This list is used to monitor such loans and is used in the determination of the sufficiency of the Company&#146;s allowance for loan losses. As of December 31, 2006, the allowance for loan losses was $2.1 million, or 1.36% of total loans, as compared to $1.6 million and $1.4 million, or 1.19%, and $1.25% in 2005 and 2004, respectively. </P>

<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px"><B>Nonperforming assets</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:5.533px; margin-bottom:5.533px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, TransCommunity had $961 thousand in nonperforming loans. &nbsp;At December 31, 2005 and 2004, TransCommunity had $165 thousand and $0, respectively, of loans classified as nonperforming. &nbsp;Loans are placed on nonaccrual status when, in the opinion of management, the collection of principal and interest are considered to be doubtful. &nbsp;No interest is accrued on loans placed in a nonaccrual status, and any unpaid interest previously accrued on such loans is reversed when a loan is placed in nonaccrual status. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><B>Allocation of the Allowance for Loan Losses</B></P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px">The allowance for loan losses consists of an allocated component and an unallocated component. &nbsp;The allocated component of the allowance for loan losses reflects expected losses resulting from analyses developed through specific allocations for individual loans. &nbsp;The unallocated portion of the allowance reflects management's estimate of probable inherent but not specifically identified losses within the portfolio. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:13.6px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px"><B>Premises and Equipment</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Premises and equipment decreased to $6.7 million at December 31, 2006 from $6.8 million at December 31, 2005, but was up from $6.1 million at December 31, 2004. This decrease for 2006 was primarily attributable to the depreciation of assets.</P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px" align=justify><B>Deposits</B></P>

<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px" align=justify><B>Capital</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>On July 22, 2005, TransCommunity completed the sale of 2.3 million shares of its common stock at $8.00 per share in a registered public offering to a limited number of institutional investors. &nbsp;The minimum share purchase in the offering was 25,000 shares. &nbsp;The offering was made through a firm commitment underwriting in which Sandler O&#146;Neill &amp; Partners, L.P. served as the sole manager. &nbsp;TransCommunity received net proceeds from the offering of approximately $16.8 million after deducting underwriting discounts and expenses. &nbsp;A portion of the net proceeds from the offering was used to repay the outstanding principal balance of $1.45 million and accrued interest on TransCommunity&#146;s line of credit. &nbsp;TransCommunity utilized $8.0 million, to provide the initial capital for Bank of Rockbridge, a new bank TransCommunity established in Rockbridge County, Virginia. &nbsp;Additionally, TransCommunity used $3.3 million of the proceeds from this offering to strengthen the capital position of two of its subsidiary banks. &nbsp;The remaining proceeds were used to accommodate future growth and for general corporate purposes, which included, among other things, operating expenses of the holding company headquarters. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>28</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>The Federal Reserve Board, the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Virginia Bureau of Financial Institutions have adopted risk-based capital measures for regulatory purposes to assist in the assessment of capital adequacy. &nbsp;Management seeks to balance the return on equity to shareholders while satisfying the regulatory standards for risk-based capital ratios. &nbsp;Management believes, as of December 31, 2006, that the Company and each of its subsidiary banks met all of the minimum regulatory capital requirements and are categorized as &#147;well capitalized&#148;. &nbsp;At December 31, 2006, the Company had a leverage ratio of 15.86%, a Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio of 17.16% and a total risk-based capital ratio of 18.32%. &nbsp;The book value of the Company&#146;s common stock at December 31, 2006 was $6.67 per share.</P>

<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px" align=justify><B>Liquidity and Interest Sensitivity</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:36px" align=justify>&#147;Liquidity&#148; measures whether an entity has sufficient cash flow to meet its financial obligation and commitments on a timely basis. TransCommunity is liquid when its subsidiary banks have the cash available to meet borrowing and cash withdrawal requirements of customers and the Bank can pay for current and planned expenditures and satisfy its debt obligations. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
