<P style="margin-top:6.933px; margin-bottom:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>At December&nbsp;31, 2006, the Company had $53.3 million of off-balance sheet credit exposure in the form of $48.3 million of commitments and $5.0 million of standby letters of credit. &nbsp;Commitments generally have fixed expiration dates or other termination clauses and may require payment of a fee. The commitments for equity lines of credit may expire without being drawn upon. &nbsp;Standby letters of credit are conditional commitments issued by the Company to guarantee the performance of a customer to a third party. The credit risk involved in issuing letters of credit is essentially the same as that involved in extending loan facilities to customers. The Company generally holds collateral supporting those commitments if deemed necessary. </P>
<P style="margin-top:6.933px; margin-bottom:0px"><B>Interest Rate Risk </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Closely related to the concept of liquidity is the concept of interest rate sensitivity (i.e., the extent to which assets and liabilities are sensitive to changes in interest rates). Interest rate sensitivity is often measured by the extent to which mismatches or &#147;gaps&#148; occur in the repricing of assets and liabilities within a given period. Gap analysis is utilized to quantify such mismatches. A &#147;positive&#148; gap results when the amount of earning assets repricing within a given time period exceeds the amount of interest-bearing liabilities repricing within that time period. A &#147;negative&#148; gap results when the amount of interest-bearing liabilities repricing within a given time period exceeds the amount of earning assets repricing within such time period. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>TransCommunity&#146;s potential interest rate volatility is a primary component of its market risk. Fluctuations in interest rates will ultimately impact the level of income and expense recorded on a large portion of the Company&#146;s assets and liabilities, and the market value of all interest-earning assets, other than those which possess a short term to maturity. Based upon the Company&#146;s nature of operations, the Company is not subject to foreign currency exchange. The Company does not own any trading assets and does not have any hedging transactions in place, such as interest rate swaps and caps.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>30</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company monitors and controls interest rate risk through a variety of techniques, including use of traditional interest rate sensitivity analysis (also known as &#147;gap analysis&#148;) Traditional gap analysis involves arranging the Company&#146;s interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities by repricing periods and then computing the difference (or &#147;interest rate sensitivity gap&#148;) between the assets and liabilities that are estimated to reprice during each time period and cumulatively through the end of each time period. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Both interest rate sensitivity modeling and gap analysis are done at a specific point in time and involve a variety of significant estimates and assumptions. Interest rate sensitivity modeling requires, among other things, estimates of how much and when yields and costs on individual categories of interest-earning assets and interest &#150;bearing liabilities will respond to general changes in market rates, future cash flows and discount rates.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Gap analysis requires estimates as to when individual categories of interest-sensitive assets and liabilities will reprice, and assumes that assets and liabilities assigned to the same repricing period will reprice at the same time and in the same amount. Gap analysis does not account for the fact that repricing of assets and liabilities is discretionary and subject to competitive and other pressures.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The schedule on the following page does not necessarily indicate the impact of general interest rate movements on the Company&#146;s net interest income because the repricing of certain categories of assets and liabilities, for example, prepayments of loans and withdrawal of deposits, is beyond the Company&#146;s control. As a result, certain assets and liabilities indicated as repricing within a stated period may in fact reprice at different times and at different levels. </P>
<P style="margin-top:6.933px; margin-bottom:0px" align=right><BR>

<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px" align=justify><B>Item 7A. </B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:96px" align=justify><B>Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Market risk is the risk of loss in a financial instrument arising from adverse changes in market rates or prices such as interest rates, foreign currency exchange rates, commodity prices and equity prices. &nbsp;The Company&#146;s primary market risk exposure is interest rate risk. &nbsp;The ongoing monitoring and management of this risk is an important component of the Company&#146;s asset/liability management process. &nbsp;The Board of Directors of each bank delegates responsibility for carrying out asset/liability management policies to the Asset/Liability Committee (&#147;ALCO&#148;) of the Bank. &nbsp;In this capacity, ALCO develops guidelines and strategies that govern the Company&#146;s asset/liability management related activities, based upon estimated market risk sensitivity, policy limits, and overall market interest rate levels and trends. Under the new consolidated entity, it is anticipated that this function will be consolidated into the single bank&#146;s operations and the board will establish the same type of ALCO committee to operate for the consolidated investment portfolio using the currently existing guidelines and procedures used by each separately chartered bank.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>34</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Interest rate risk represents the sensitivity of earnings to changes in market interest rates. &nbsp;As interest rates change, the interest income and expense streams associated with the Company&#146;s financial instruments also change, affecting net interest income, the primary component of the Company&#146;s earnings. &nbsp;The flat yield curve that currently exists, has existed now for several years and has forced the banks&#146; ALCO committees to focus on maintaining a short maturity highly liquid portfolio with a high level of floating investments. This portfolio structure is also necessary to maintain the liquidity for a growing loan portfolio experienced by most of our banking subsidiaries. The chart below summarized the estimated impact on net interest income from interest rate changes as listed based on earning assets and interest bearing liabilities for the years ended 2006 and 2005.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16px" align=justify><B>Item 9A.</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:60px" align=justify><B>Controls and Procedures</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Disclosure Controls and Procedures</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company is required to maintain disclosure controls and procedures that are designed to provide reasonable assurance that information required to be disclosed in reports filed under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the &#147;Exchange Act&#148;), such as this annual report on Form 10-K, is recorded, processed, summarized and reported within the time periods specified in the rules and forms of the Securities and Exchange Commission, and that such information is accumulated and communicated to its management, including its principal executive officer and principal financial officer, as appropriate, to allow timely decisions regarding required disclosure. In designing and evaluating the disclosure controls and procedures, the Company recognizes that any controls and procedures, no matter how well designed and operated, can provide only reasonable assurance of achieving the desired control objectives, and management necessarily is required to apply its judgment in evaluating the cost-benefit relationship of possible controls and procedures.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR>
<BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=center>35</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<HR style="margin-top:9.6px; margin-bottom:9.6px" noshade size=1.333>
<P style="margin:0px; page-break-before:always" align=right><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>The Company conducted an evaluation under the supervision and with the participation of our management, including our Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer, of the effectiveness of the design and operation of our disclosure controls and procedures (as defined in Rule 13a-15(e) under the Exchange Act) as of December&nbsp;31, 2006. Based upon that evaluation, our Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer concluded that the Company&#146;s disclosure controls and procedures were not effective as of December 31, 2006. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><B>Internal Control over Financial Reporting</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Our management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting (as defined in Rules&nbsp;13a-15(f) under the Exchange Act) for the Company. This system is designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>As more fully described in Note&nbsp;25 of the Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements, we discovered accounting errors in our previously reported financial results for 2005 and concluded on August 10, 2006 that the related financial statements would need to be restated due to the determination that there was a material weakness in our internal control over financial reporting. &nbsp;A material weakness is a control deficiency, or combination of control deficiencies, that results in more than a remote likelihood that a material misstatement of the annual or interim financial statements will not be prevented or detected. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>In recognition of the accounting issues noted above, we are centralizing certain operational areas to provide a clearer segregation of responsibilities in connection with loan origination and monitoring activities. &nbsp;The Company contracted a third party consulting firm to help the Company analyze its alternatives and implement recommended process improvements. &nbsp;The Company received the consultant&#146;s recommendations at the end of January 2007. &nbsp;Following receipt of the report of the consultant, the Company&#146;s Board of Directors voted to consolidate its existing bank charters into a single legal entity.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>As a part of the Company&#146;s preparation for compliance with the requirements of Section&nbsp;404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, the Company will continue to evaluate the effectiveness of its internal controls and procedures on an ongoing basis and will take further action as appropriate. Section&nbsp;404 will require the Company&#146;s management to report on the effectiveness of the Company&#146;s internal control structure and procedures for financial reporting as of December&nbsp;31, 2007. Future remedial measures that we are considering include organizational changes to improve supervision and increased training for operations and accounting personnel. We will continue to develop new policies and procedures and educate and train our employees on our existing policies and procedures in our effort to constantly improve our internal controls and control environment.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; text-indent:48px" align=justify>Other than as described above, there were no changes in the Company&#146;s internal control over financial reporting in the quarter ended December&nbsp;31, 2006, that materially affected, or are reasonably likely to materially affect, the Company&#146;s internal control over financial reporting. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="margin:0px">We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheets of TransCommunity Financial Corporation and Subsidiaries as of December 31, 2006 and 2005, and the related consolidated statements of operations, changes in stockholders equity and cash flows for the years then ended. These financial statements are the responsibility of the Company&#146;s management. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audits.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px">We conducted our audits in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States). Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. An audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall financial statement presentation. We believe that our audits provide a reasonable basis for our opinion.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px">In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position of TransCommunity Financial Corporation and Subsidiaries as of December 31, 2006 and 2005, and the results of their operations and their cash flows for the years ended, in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px">As discussed in Note 2 to the consolidated financial statements, in 2006 TransCommunity Financial Corporation and Subsidiaries adopted Statement of Financial Accounting Standards No. 123R, Share-Based Payment.</P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>TRANSCOMMUNITY FINANCIAL CORPORATION</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=justify><B>NOTE 1 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;NATURE OF OPERATIONS:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>TransCommunity Financial Corporation (&#147;TransCommunity&#148; or the &#147;Company&#148;) is a bank holding company whose principal activity is the formation, ownership and operation of independently-managed community banks. TransCommunity&#146;s first subsidiary, the Bank of Powhatan, N.A. (&#147;Bank of Powhatan&#148;), was organized as a national banking association in 1999, and commenced operations on March 20, 2000. &nbsp;TransCommunity&#146;s second subsidiary, Bank of Goochland, N.A. (&#147;Bank of Goochland&#148;), was organized and incorporated during 2002, and commenced operations on November 25, 2002. &nbsp;On April 19, 2004, TransCommunity established its third independent community bank in the central Virginia area, the Bank of Louisa, N.A. (&#147;Bank of Louisa&#148;), TransCommunity initially established the Bank of Louisa in July 2003 as a branch of Bank of Powhatan. &nbsp;The assets and liabilities of this branch office were transferred to Bank of Louisa contemporaneously with the receipt by that bank of its independent national banking charter in April 2004. &nbsp;On December 11, 2006, TransCommunity commenced the operations of the Bank of Rockbridge, its fourth subsidiary bank (&#147;Bank of Rockbridge&#148; together with Bank of Powhatan, Bank of Goochland, and Bank of Louisa, the &#147;banks&#148;.)</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>TransCommunity&#146;s subsidiary banks are subject to regulation by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Virginia Bureau of Financial Institution, and the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. &nbsp;The banks provide general banking services to individuals, small- and medium-size businesses and the professional communities of Powhatan, Goochland, Rockbridge, and Louisa Counties of Virginia and surrounding areas. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>On January 1, 2001, the Bank of Powhatan purchased Main Street Mortgage and Investment Corporation (&#147;Main Street&#148;) which became a wholly-owned subsidiary of the bank. &nbsp;Main Street originated commercial and residential real estate loans for investors throughout the state. &nbsp;However, in November of 2006, the Board of Directors voted to discontinue the operations of Main Street.</P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>During 2004, TransCommunity applied for and received authority to offer trust services through each of its national bank subsidiaries. &nbsp;TransCommunity Investment Advisors, Inc., an investment advisory subsidiary, was formed to handle asset management and TransCommunity Investment Services, an insurance agency and investment broker, was established to broaden the scope of financial services available through each of the subsidiary banks. &nbsp;During the fourth quarter of 2005, the Board of Directors directed management to discontinue the operations of these non-bank activities.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:17.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-17.333px" align=justify><B>NOTE 2</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><BR>
Basis of financial presentation - The accounting and reporting policies of the Company and its subsidiaries conform to accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (US GAAP) and predominant practices within the banking industry. &nbsp;The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of the Company and its wholly-owned subsidiaries. All significant intercompany accounts and transactions have been eliminated.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The preparation of financial statements requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements. &nbsp;These estimates and assumptions also affect reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. &nbsp;Actual results could differ from those estimates. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The principal estimate that is particularly susceptible to significant change in the near term relates to the allowance for loan losses. The evaluation of the adequacy of the allowance for loan losses includes an analysis of the individual loans and overall risk characteristics and size of the different loan portfolios, and takes into consideration current economic and market conditions, the capability of specific borrowers to pay specific loan obligations, and current loan collateral values. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>In connection with the determination of the estimated losses on loans, management obtains independent appraisals for significant collateral. &nbsp;Actual losses on specific loans, which also are encompassed in the analysis, may vary from estimated losses.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Principles of consolidation</B> - The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of the Company, which is a bank holding company that owns all of the outstanding common stock of its banking subsidiaries, Bank of Powhatan, Bank of Goochland, Bank of Louisa, Bank of Rockbridge, and Main Street Mortgage and Investment Corporation, Inc., a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bank of Powhatan. &nbsp;All significant inter-company balances and transactions have been eliminated.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>TRANSCOMMUNITY FINANCIAL CORPORATION</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:17.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-17.333px" align=justify><B>NOTE 2</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (Continued):</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Business segments</B> - SFAS&nbsp;No.&nbsp;131, &#147;Disclosures about Segments of an Enterprise and Related Information&#148; establishes standards for the way public business enterprises report information about operating segments in annual financial statements and requires that those enterprises report selected information about operating segments in interim financial reports issued to shareholders. It also establishes standards for related disclosure about products and services, geographic areas, and major customers. Operating segments are components of an enterprise about which separate financial information is available that is evaluated regularly by the chief operating decision maker in deciding how to allocate resources and assess performance. The statement also requires that public enterprises report a measure of segment profit or loss, certain specific revenue and expense items and segment assets. It also requires that information be reported about revenues derived from the enterprises&#146; products or services, or about the countries in which the enterprises earn revenues and hold assets, and about major customers, regardless of whether the information is used in making operating decisions. The accounting policies of the segments are the same as those described in this Note. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Management has determined that the Company has two current reportable segments, &#147;Community Banking and TransCommunity (the holding company).&#148; All of the Company&#146;s subsidiary banks&#146; activities are interrelated, and each of their activities is dependent and assessed based on how each of the subsidiary bank&#146;s consolidated activities for the Company supports the others. For example, commercial lending is dependent upon the ability of the subsidiary banks to fund themselves with retail deposits and other borrowings and to manage interest rate and credit risk. This situation is also similar for consumer and residential mortgage lending. Accordingly, all significant operating decisions are based upon analysis of the consolidated operations of the subsidiary banks as a consolidated segment. The current operations of the holding company are identified as a segment due to their consolidated support services supplied to the subsidiary banks and the cost related to those support services as an operating unit. </P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The Company has also reported in the past several operating segments that have been discontinued. These discontinued operating segments within the Company&#146;s operations, although no longer in existence, will be segregated for comparative reasons and to identify the discontinued operations impact on the company&#146;s past operations. </P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The financial statement information of the parent company is included as a reportable segment. &nbsp;This segment is principally involved with providing managerial support and the operation of the shared services platform for the other reportable segments.</P>

<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><BR>
<B>Investment securities - </B>The Company accounts for its investment securities in accordance with SFAS No.115, <I>Accounting for Certain Investments in Debt and Equity Securities</I>. &nbsp;Investment securities that the Company has the ability and intent to hold to maturity are classified as held-to-maturity and are stated at cost, adjusted for premium amortization and discount accretion. &nbsp;Securities which are held for indefinite periods of time which management intends to use as part of its asset/liability management strategy, or that may be sold in response to changes in interest rates, changes in prepayment risk, increased capital requirements or other similar factors, are classified as available-for-sale and are carried at fair market value. Net unrealized gains and losses for such securities, net of income tax effect, are charged/credited directly to accumulated other comprehensive income (loss), a component of shareholders&#146; equity. Securities transactions are accounted for on a trade date basis. Gains or losses on disposition of investment securities are based on the net proceeds and the adjusted carrying amount of the securities sold using the specific identification method.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>As of December 31, 2006 and 2005, the Company did not have any foreign investment securities or securities designated as trading account investments. </P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>TRANSCOMMUNITY FINANCIAL CORPORATION</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:17.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-17.333px" align=justify><B>NOTE 2</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (Continued):</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>SFAS No.133, <I>Accounting for Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activity</I>, established accounting and reporting standards for derivative instruments, including certain derivative instruments embedded in other contracts, and for hedging activities. &nbsp;It requires that an entity recognize all derivatives as either assets or liabilities in the statement of financial position and measure those instruments at fair value. SFAS No.133 was amended by SFAS No.138, <I>Accounting for Certain Derivative Instruments and Certain Hedging Activities</I>. The Company&#146;s adoption of SFAS No.133, as amended, did not have a material impact on its financial condition or results of operations. The Company did not have any derivatives at December 31, 2006 and 2005.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The Company adopted EITF 03-1, <I>The Meaning of Other than Temporary Impairment and Its Application to Certain Investments</I>, as of December 31, 2003.&nbsp; EITF 03-1 includes certain required quantitative and qualitative disclosures for investment securities accounted for under SFAS No. 115, <I>Accounting for Certain Investments in Debt and Equity Securities</I>, that are impaired at the balance sheet date, but an other-than-temporary impairment has not been recognized.&nbsp; In November 2005, the FASB issued Staff Position FSP No. FAS 115-1 and FAS 124-1, <I>The Meaning of Other-Than-Temporary Impairment and Its Application to Certain Investments</I>. This FSP provides guidance on determining when an investment is considered impaired, whether that impairment is other than temporary, and the measurement of an impairment loss. &nbsp;The FSP also provides accounting considerations subsequent to the recognition of an other-than-temporary impairment and requires certain disclosures about unrealized losses that have not been recognized as other-than-temporary impairments. &nbsp;&nbsp;The Company adopted FSP No. FAS 115-1 and FAS 124-1 as of December 31, 2005. The disclosures required under EITF 03-1 and FSP No. FAS 115-1 and FAS 124-1 are included in these consolidated financial statements.</P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Loans and allowance for loan losses - </B>Loans that management has the intent and the ability to hold for the foreseeable future or until maturity or payoff are stated at the amount of unpaid principal net of unearned discount, unamortized loan fees and loan origination costs and an allowance for loan losses. &nbsp;The allowance for loan losses is established through a provision for loan losses charged to expense. &nbsp;Loans are charged against the allowance for loan losses when management believes that the collectibility of principal is unlikely. The allowance for loan losses is maintained at a level that management considers adequate to provide for credit losses inherent in the loan portfolios at the reporting date. The level of the allowance is based on management&#146;s evaluation of risk of loss in the loan portfolios after consideration of prevailing and anticipated economic conditions, including estimates and appraisals, among other items, known or anticipated at each reporting date. On a periodic basis during the year, management makes credit reviews of the loan portfolios designed to identify &nbsp;any changes in the loans since initial booking impacting their &nbsp;quality rating. &nbsp;This review is designed to identify potential changes to the loan loss reserve.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Interest income on loans is credited to operations based upon the principal amount outstanding. &nbsp;The net amounts of origination fees, origination costs and commitment fees are deferred and recognized over the lives of the related loans and leases as adjustments of yield. &nbsp;When management believes there is sufficient doubt as to the ultimate collectibility of interest on any loan, the accrual of applicable interest is discontinued. &nbsp;A loan is generally classified as nonaccrual when principal and interest have consistently been in default for a period of 90 days or more or because of deterioration in the financial condition of the borrower, and payment in full of principal or interest is not expected. &nbsp;Loans past due 90 days or more and still accruing interest are loans that are generally well-secured and expected to be restored to a current status in the near future or are in the process of collection. &nbsp;In all cases, loans are placed on nonaccrual or are charged off at an earlier date if collection of principal or interest is considered doubtful. </P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>All interest accrued but not collected for loans that are placed on nonaccrual or charged off is reversed against interest income. &nbsp;The interest on these loans is accounted for on the cash-basis or cost-recovery method, until qualifying for return to accrual. &nbsp;Loans are returned to accrual status when all the principal and interest amounts contractually due are brought current and future payments are reasonably assured.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The Company follows SFAS No.114, <I>Accounting by Creditors for Impairment of a Loan</I>, as amended by SFAS No.118, <I>Accounting by Creditors for Impairment of a Loan &#150; Income Recognition and Disclosures</I>. &nbsp;This standard requires that certain impaired loans be measured based on the present value of expected future cash flows discounted at the loan&#146;s effective interest rates, except that as a practical expedient, a creditor may measure impairment based on a loan&#146;s observable market price, or the fair value of the collateral if the loan is collateral dependent. &nbsp;Regardless of the measurement method, a creditor must measure impairment based on the fair value of the collateral when the creditor determines that foreclosure is probable.</P>

<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>TRANSCOMMUNITY FINANCIAL CORPORATION</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:17.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-17.333px" align=justify><B>NOTE 2</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (Continued):</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Premises and equipment - </B>Premises and equipment are stated at cost less accumulated depreciation and amortization. &nbsp;Depreciation is computed primarily on the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets. Leasehold improvements are amortized over the term of the lease or estimated useful life, whichever is shorter. </P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The Company follows SFAS No.144, <I>Accounting for the Impairment or Disposal of Long-Lived Assets</I>. &nbsp;SFAS No.144 retained the existing requirements to recognize and measure the impairment of long-lived assets to be held and used or to be disposed of by sale. SFAS No.144 also changed the requirements relating to reporting the effects of a disposal or discontinuation of a segment of a business. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:13.333px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Transfers of Financial Assets</B> - The Company follows SFAS No. 140, &#147;Accounting for Transfers and Servicing of Financial Assets and Extinguishments of Liabilities - a replacement of SFAS No. 125&#148; (&#147;Statement 140&#148;). &nbsp;Transfers of financial assets are accounted for as sales when control over the assets has been surrendered. &nbsp;Control over transferred assets is deemed to be surrendered when (1) the assets have been isolated from the Company, (2) the transferee obtains the right (free of conditions that constrain it from taking advantage of that right) to pledge or exchange the transferred assets, and (3) the Company does not maintain effective control over the transferred assets through an agreement to repurchase them before their maturity.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Goodwill and intangible assets - </B>SFAS No.&nbsp;141, <I>Business Combinations,</I> requires that the purchase method of accounting be used for all business combinations.. For purchase acquisitions, the Company is required to record assets acquired, including identifiable intangible assets, and liabilities assumed at their fair value, which in many instances involves estimates based on third party valuations, such as appraisals, or internal valuations based on discounted cash flow analysis or other valuation techniques. SFAS No.&nbsp;142, <I>Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets, </I>prescribes the accounting for goodwill and intangible assets subsequent to initial recognition. The provisions of SFAS No.&nbsp;142 discontinue the amortization of goodwill and intangible assets with indefinite lives but require at least an annual impairment review, and more frequently if certain impairment indicators are in evidence. The Company adopted SFAS 147, <I>Acquisitions of Certain Financial Institutions,</I> on January&nbsp;1, 2002 and determined that core deposit intangibles will continue to be amortized over the estimated useful life.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Income taxes - </B>The Company accounts for income taxes under the liability method. &nbsp;Under this method, deferred tax assets and liabilities are determined based on the difference between the financial statement and tax bases of assets and liabilities as measured by the enacted tax rates that expects to be in effect when these differences reverse. Deferred tax expense is the result of changes in deferred tax assets and liabilities. &nbsp;The principal types of accounts resulting in differences between assets and liabilities for financial statement and tax return purposes are the allowance for loan losses, interest income on nonaccrual loans, depreciation and amortization, difference between book and tax bases of assets acquired and net operating loss carryforwards. The Company and its subsidiaries file a consolidated federal income tax return.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Statements of cash flows - </B>Cash and cash equivalents are defined as the sum of cash on hand, non interest-bearing amounts due from banks and federal funds sold. &nbsp;Generally, federal funds are sold for a one-day period. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Other real estate owned - </B>Other real estate owned is recorded at lower of cost or market value less costs of disposal. &nbsp;When property is acquired, the excess, if any, of the loan balance over fair market value is charged to the allowance for loan losses. &nbsp;Periodically thereafter, the asset is reviewed for subsequent declines in the estimated fair market value. &nbsp;Subsequent declines, if any, holding costs and gains and losses on subsequent sale are included in the consolidated statements of operations. &nbsp;At December 31, 2006 and 2005, the Company held no other real estate owned.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Marketing costs - </B>The Company expenses marketing costs as incurred. &nbsp;Marketing expenses for the years ended December 31, 2006, 2005, and 2004 were approximately $221 thousand, $428 thousand and $373 thousand, respectively.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Earnings per share - </B>Basic earnings per share excludes dilution and is computed by dividing income available to common shareholders by the weighted average common shares outstanding during the period. &nbsp;Diluted earnings per share takes into account the potential dilution that could occur if stock options or other contracts to issue common stock were exercised and converted into common stock. &nbsp;Stock options for 241,725, 256,325 and 317,375 shares of common stock were not considered in computing diluted earnings per share for 2006, 2005 and 2004, respectively, because they were antidilutive.</P>

<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (Continued):</B></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Stock based compensation -</B>In December 2004, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (&#147;FASB&#148;) issued Statement of Financial Accounting Standards (&#147;SFAS&#148;) No.&nbsp;123R, &#147;Share-Based Payment,&#148; that addresses the accounting for share-based payment transactions in which an enterprise exchanges its equity instruments for goods and services. The Statement eliminates the ability to account for share-based compensation transactions using Accounting Principles Board (&#147;APB&#148;) Opinion No.&nbsp;25, &#147;Accounting for Stock Issued to Employees,&#148; and requires instead that such transactions be accounted for using a fair-value-based method. &nbsp;SFAS No. 123R required implementation by the beginning of the first fiscal year that begins after June&nbsp;15, 2005. On January&nbsp;1, 2006, TransCommunity implemented SFAS No. 123R using the modified prospective transition method. &nbsp;By implementing SFAS No. 123R, TransCommunity recorded $31 thousand of additional compensation expense during the year ended December 31, 2006, resulting from the application of fair-value-based accounting to its stock-based compensation programs. See Note 16 for more information about TransCommunity&#146;s stock-based compensation programs. </P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Comprehensive income (loss) - </B>The Company follows the disclosure provisions of SFAS No.130, Reporting Comprehensive Income. &nbsp;SFAS No. 130 requires the reporting of comprehensive income which includes net income (loss) as well as certain other items that result in a change to shareholders&#146; equity during the period.</P>
<P style="margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Reclassifications and restatements</B> - Certain reclassifications have been made in the 2004 and 2005 financial statements to conform to the classifications used in 2006. &nbsp;Additionally, certain restatements were made to 2005 and 2004 financial statements as discussed in Note 25.</P>
<P style="line-height:13.867px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>New Accounting Pronouncements</B> &#150; In May 2005, the FASB issued Statement No.&nbsp;154, &#147;<I>Accounting Changes and Error Corrections&nbsp;&#151;&nbsp;a replacement of APB Opinion No.&nbsp;20 and FASB Statement No.&nbsp;3</I>&#148; (&#147;SFAS&nbsp;154&#148;). &nbsp;SFAS&nbsp;154 changes the accounting for and reporting of a voluntary change in accounting principle and replaces ABP Opinion No.&nbsp;20, &#147;<I>Accounting Changes</I>&#148; and FASB Statement No.&nbsp;3, &#147;<I>Reporting Accounting Changes in Interim Financial Statements</I>.&#148; Under Opinion No.&nbsp;20, most changes in accounting principle were reported in the income statement of the period of change as a cumulative adjustment. However, under SFAS&nbsp;154, a voluntary change in accounting principle must be shown retrospectively in the financial statements, if practicable, for all periods presented. In cases where retrospective application is impracticable, an adjustment to the assets, liabilities and a corresponding adjustment to retained earnings can be made as of the beginning of the earliest period for which retrospective application is practicable rather than being reported in the income statement. SFAS&nbsp;154 is effective for accounting changes and corrections of errors made in fiscal years after December&nbsp;15, 2005. &nbsp;The Company does not anticipate this revision will have a material effect on its financial position or results of operations.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>In February 2006, FASB issued SFAS No. 155, &#147;<I>Accounting for Certain Hybrid Financial Instruments - an Amendment of FASB Statements No. 133 and 140</I>&#148; (&#147;SFAS 155&#148;). &nbsp;SFAS 155 amends FASB Statements No. 133, &#147;Accounting for Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities&#148;, and No. 140, &#147;Accounting for Transfers and Servicing of Financial Assets and Extinguishments of Liabilities&#148;. &nbsp;SFAS 155 resolves issues addressed in Statement 133 Implementation Issue No. D1, &#147;Application of Statement 133 to Beneficial Interests in Securitized Financial Assets.&#148; &nbsp;SFAS 155 provides a fair value measurement option for certain hybrid financial instruments that contain an embedded derivative that would otherwise require bifurcation. &nbsp;Adoption of SFAS 155 is required as of the beginning of the first fiscal year beginning subsequent to September 15, 2006. &nbsp;The Company does not anticipate the adoption of SFAS 155 in January 2007 will have a material effect on its financial position or results of operations.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>In March 2006, FASB issued SFAS No.&nbsp;156, &#147;<I>Accounting for Servicing of Financial Assets - an Amendment of FASB Statement No. 140</I>&#148; (&#147;SFAS&nbsp;156&#148;). &nbsp;SFAS 156 amends FASB Statement No. 140, &#147;Accounting for Transfers and Servicing of Financial Assets and Extinguishments of Liabilities&#148;, with respect to the accounting for separately recognized servicing assets and servicing liabilities. &nbsp;SFAS 156 requires an entity to recognize a servicing asset or servicing liability each time it undertakes an obligation to service a financial asset by entering into a servicing contract to be initially measured at fair value, if practicable. SFAS 156 also permits entities to&nbsp;subsequently measure servicing assets and liabilities using an amortization method or fair value measurement method. &nbsp;Under the amortization method, servicing assets and liabilities&nbsp;are amortized in proportion to and over the estimated period of servicing. &nbsp;Under the fair value measurement method, servicing assets are measured at fair value at each reporting date and changes in fair value are reported in net income for the period during which the change occurs. &nbsp;Adoption of SFAS 156 is required as of the beginning of the first fiscal year beginning subsequent to September 15, 2006. &nbsp;Earlier adoption is permitted as of the beginning of an entity&#146;s fiscal year, provided the entity has not yet issued financial statements, including interim financial statements, for any period of that fiscal year. &nbsp;The Company does not anticipate the adoption of SFAS 156 in January 2007 will have a material effect on its financial position or results of operations.</P>

<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (Continued):</B></P>

<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>In September 2006, the FASB released SFAS No. 157, &#147;<I>Fair Value Measurement</I>&#148;, which provides guidance for using fair value to measure assets and liabilities. SFAS No. 157 defines fair value, establishes a framework for measuring fair value in generally accepted accounting principles, and expands disclosures about fair value measurements. The standard also responds to investors&#146; requests for more information about the extent to which companies&#146; measure assets and liabilities at fair value, the information used to measure fair value and the effect that fair value measurements have on earnings. SFAS No. 157 will apply whenever another standard requires (or permits) assets or liabilities to be measured at fair value. The standard does not expand the use of fair value to any new circumstances. SFAS No. 157 is effective for financial statements issued for financial years beginning after November 15, 2007, and interim periods within those years. SFAS No. 157 is effective for the Company for years beginning after January 1, 2008, and interim periods within that year. The Company is in the process of evaluating the impact that the adoption of SFAS No. 157 will have on its consolidated financial position and results of operations.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.267px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>In June 2006, FASB issued <A NAME="CFNLANA:1134.7-1"></A>Interpretation No. 48, &#147;<I>Accounting for Uncertainty in Income Taxes&#148;</I> (<A NAME="CFNLANA:1134.2-1"></A>FIN 48). <A NAME="CFNLANA:1134.3-1"></A>FIN 48 clarifies the accounting for uncertainty in income taxes recognized in an enterprise's financial statements in accordance with <A NAME="CFNLANA:1134.8-1"></A>FASB Statement No. 109, <I>&#147;Accounting for Income Taxes.&#148;</I> <A NAME="CFNLANA:1134.4-1"></A>FIN 48 prescribes a recognition threshold and measurement attribute for the financial statement recognition and measurement of a tax position taken or expected to be taken in a tax return. This interpretation also provides guidance on derecognition, classification, interest and penalties, accounting in interim periods, disclosure, and transition. <A NAME="CFNLANA:1134.5-1"></A>FIN 48 is effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2006. Earlier application of the provisions of this interpretation is encouraged if the enterprise has not yet issued financial statements, including interim statements, in the period this interpretation is adopted. TransCommunity has evaluated FIN 48 and concluded that the adoption of this interpretation will have no material impact on its financial statements.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<A NAME="HIT1"></A><P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>In February 2007, the FASB issued SFAS No. 159 &quot;<I>The Fair Value Option for Financial Assets and Financial Liabilities</I>.&quot; This standard permits entities to choose to measure many financial instruments and certain other items at fair value. &nbsp;Unrealized gains and losses on items for which the fair value option has been elected are reported in earnings. &nbsp;&nbsp;This Statement is effective as of the beginning of an entity&#146;s first fiscal year beginning after November 15, 2007. &nbsp;Early adoption is permitted as of the beginning of the fiscal year that begins on or before November 15, 2007, provided the entity also elects to apply the provisions of SFAS 157 &#147;<I>Fair Value Measurement</I>.&#148; The Company is<A NAME="HIT2"></A> currently in the process of evaluating the impact that the adoption will have on its consolidated financial position and results of operations.</P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>TRANSCOMMUNITY FINANCIAL CORPORATION</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:18px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-18px" align=justify><B>NOTE 4</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.333px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>INVESTMENT SECURITIES (Continued):</B></P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The 2006 unrealized loss is the aggregate of 20 U.S. Agency notes, of which 11 have a continuous loss period of more than 12 months. &nbsp;The 2005 unrealized loss is the aggregate of 18 U.S. Agency notes, of which 11 have a continuous loss period of more than 12 months. &nbsp;The unrealized loss positions in both years were primarily related to interest rate movements as there is minimal credit risk exposure in these investments. All securities are investment grade or better. &nbsp;No impairment loss has been recognized on these securities because management has both the intent and the ability to hold these securities until maturity or call dates. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Management evaluates securities for other-than-temporary impairment at least on a quarterly basis and more frequently when economic or market concerns warrant such evaluation. &nbsp;Consideration is given to (1) the length of time and the extent to which the fair value has been less than cost, (2) the financial condition and near-term prospects of the issuer, and (3) the intent and ability of TransCommunity&#146;s subsidiary banks to retain its investment in the issuer for a period of time sufficient to allow for any anticipated recovery in fair value.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The carrying amount (which approximates fair value) of securities pledged by the banks to secure public deposits amounted to $11.3 million and $11.8 million at December 31, 2006 and 2005, respectively.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>TransCommunity&#146;s subsidiary banks are required to hold stock in the Federal Reserve Bank. &nbsp;The investment in Federal Reserve Bank stock is recorded at cost of $831 thousand and $536 thousand as of December 31, 2006 and 2005, respectively. &nbsp;The Company also held $65 thousand in Virginia Bankers Association Title Insurance Company Stock at year end 2006, which are classified as &#147;Other Investments&#148; in the Consolidated Balance Sheet.</P>

<P style="line-height:17.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-17.333px" align=justify><B>NOTE 9</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>NOTES PAYABLE AND SECURED BORROWINGS:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Notes Payable - </B>On July 21, 2006, Main Street Mortgage and Financial Corporation entered into a $500 thousand unsecured revolving line of credit fully guaranteed by TransCommunity. &nbsp;This fully drawn line of credit, due upon demand, required monthly interest only payments based on the prime rate as published by the <I>Wall Street Journal</I>, which was 8.25% at December 31, 2006. &nbsp;Interest was paid as agreed by Main Street until year-end 2006, when it discontinued operations and TransCommunity assumed the note. &nbsp;During 2006, interest expense associated with this line of credit was $18 thousand and is included in the results of discontinued operations. &nbsp;Starting January 2007, Transcommunity continued interest payments until March 2007, when the note was paid in full. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>Secured Borrowings - </B>Secured borrowings amounted to $12.5 million at December 31, 2005. Pursuant to SFAS Statement 140, certain loan participation agreements did not qualify for sale accounting due to buyback provisions included within the agreement, thus the Company had not surrendered control over the transferred loans and had accounted for the transfers as secured borrowings. &nbsp;During September 2006, the Company amended all participation loan agreements such that as of September 29, 2006, all loan participation agreements became eligible for sale accounting in accordance with Statement 140 and as a result the secured borrowings were short-term in nature.</P>

<B>NOTE 10</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>CAPITAL STOCK:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>TransCommunity is authorized to issue up to 25,000,000 shares of common stock, $.01 par value per share, and up to 5,000,000 shares of preferred stock, $.01 par value per share. &nbsp;At December 31, 2006 and December 31, 2005 TransCommunity had 4,581,741 shares of common stock issued and outstanding, respectively. &nbsp;On the same dates no shares of preferred stock were issued or outstanding.</P>
<P style="margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>During the period June 2004 to February 2005, TransCommunity sold 225,528 shares of common stock in a non-underwritten public offering, at a purchase price of $15 per share. &nbsp;Additionally, 100 shares of common stock were issued in 2005 in connection with an option exercise by one option holder. &nbsp;These shares were issued at an option exercise price of $10.00 per share. &nbsp;In July 2005, TransCommunity sold 2,300,000 shares of common stock in an underwritten public offering to a limited number of institutional investors at a purchase price of $8.00 per share. &nbsp;The minimum share purchase requirement in the offering was 25,000 shares per investor.</P>
<P style="margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="margin:0px; padding-left:72px">In November 2005, TransCommunity repurchased 11,500 shares of common stock sold in the 2004-2005 non-underwritten offering from one person residing in a jurisdiction in which such shares had not been properly registered for sale. &nbsp;The shares were repurchased at the original issue price at $15 per share.</P>
<P style="line-height:16.8px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:17.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-17.333px" align=justify><B>NOTE 11</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>DIVIDEND LIMITATIONS:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>A principal source of funds for TransCommunity in future years is anticipated to be dividends paid by its subsidiary banks. Dividends paid by the banks are limited by banking regulations. Approval of the Comptroller of the Currency is required if the dividends declared by a national bank, in any year, exceed the sum of (1) net income for the current year and (2) income, net of dividends, for the preceding two years. &nbsp;No dividends were paid to TransCommunity in 2006.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>In January of 2007, the Bank of Powhatan and the Bank of Goochland each paid TransCommunity a $300 thousand dividend out of their respective retained earnings.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>TransCommunity may not pay a dividend while there is an accumulated deficit.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>TRANSCOMMUNITY FINANCIAL CORPORATION</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:17.333px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-17.333px; padding-left:72px; text-indent:-48px" align=justify><B>NOTE 12</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px; text-indent:24px" align=justify><B>INCOME TAXES (Continued):</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>At December 31, 2006, TransCommunity had total net operating loss carryforwards of $7.5 million which begin to expire after December 31, 2020. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>For the year ended December 31, 2006, TransCommunity generated taxable income of $1 million which is fully offset by available net operating losses generated in prior years. &nbsp;However, as a result of a 90% limitation with respect to deducting alternative minimum tax net operating loss carryovers, TransCommunity&#146;s current expense for income taxes for the year ended December 31, 2006 is $15 thousand in alternative minimum tax. &nbsp;TransCommunity may be subject to the alternative minimum tax in future years. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The net deferred tax assets at December 31, 2006 and 2005, consisted primarily of the tax effect of net operating loss carryforwards incurred in years after December 31, 2000. &nbsp;The net deferred tax assets recognized, at December 31, 2006 and 2005, are fully offset by a valuation allowance since, at this time, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that TransCommunity will produce continuing and sufficient taxable income in the future to utilize its net operating losses and other deductible temporary differences.</P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The Company issued common stock in 2002 and 2005 resulting in a more than 50% change in ownership. &nbsp;As a result, utilization of certain of the Company's net operating losses incurred in the periods prior to the changes are limited under Internal Revenue Code &#167;382 as to the amount that can be used to offset taxable income in subsequent years. &nbsp;In 2005, the Company incurred approximately $656 thousand of net operating loss after the change of control. &nbsp;&nbsp;Taxable income in future years that exceed the annual &#167;382 limit and the post change of control net operating loss will be taxed at regular corporate tax rates.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:18.133px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-18.133px" align=justify><B>NOTE 13</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.467px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>CONCENTRATION OF CREDIT RISK:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.467px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Most of the banks&#146; loans are made to customers in the banks&#146; trade areas. &nbsp;Accordingly, the ultimate collectibility of the banks&#146; loan portfolio is susceptible to changes in local economic conditions. &nbsp;The types of loans made by the banks are described in Note 5. &nbsp;Collateral required by the banks is determined on an individual basis depending on the nature of the loan and the financial condition of the borrower. &nbsp;TransCommunity has a concentration of loans secured by real estate. &nbsp;At December 31, 2006, real estate loans represented 73.3% of the loans in the consolidated portfolio. Real estate lending by the banks generally consists of commercial real estate loans, construction and development loans, and residential and home equity loans. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The Company maintains deposits at other high credit quality commercial banks that may, at times, exceed federally insured limits.</P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>TRANSCOMMUNITY FINANCIAL CORPORATION</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.467px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:18.133px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-18.133px; padding-left:72px; text-indent:-72px" align=justify><B>NOTE 15</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.467px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify><B>GOODWILL: </B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.467px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>During the second quarter of 2006, TransCommunity completed an impairment test of its goodwill in accordance with the specific requirements of SFAS No. 142 &#147;<I>Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets</I>&#148;. &nbsp;This Statement addresses financial accounting and reporting for acquired goodwill and other intangible assets and supersedes APB Opinion No. 17, &#147;Intangible Assets&#148;. It addresses how intangible assets that are acquired individually or with a group of other assets should be accounted for in financial statements upon their acquisition. This Statement also addresses how goodwill and other intangible assets should be accounted for after they have been initially recognized in the financial statements. &nbsp;Based on second quarter personnel changes and a continued deterioration of the financial condition of Main Street Mortgage, the Company believed the $321 thousand of goodwill reported as other assets associated with the acquisition of Main Street Mortgage should be tested for impairment. &nbsp;The Company used a valuation approach which included comparisons of historical forecasts to actual results and earnings forecasts for the next year to determine if the fair value of the subsidiary exceeded </P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>the book value. &nbsp;Because goodwill is defined as the excess of the cost of an acquired entity over the fair value of all identifiable tangible and intangible assets acquired and the liabilities assumed, the Company was required to calculate the fair value of such assets and liabilities for Main Street. &nbsp;Through this process, the Company concluded that the entire $321 thousand of goodwill was impaired and this amount was charged to operating expenses during the second quarter of 2006.</P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:18.133px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-18.133px" align=justify><B>NOTE 16</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.467px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px" align=justify><B>STOCK OPTION PLAN:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Under the Company&#146;s Stock Option Plan (the &#147;Plan&#148;), the Company may grant options to its directors, officers and employees for up to 330,000 of common stock. &nbsp;Annual grants of stock options are limited to 10,000 shares for each employee and 7,500 shares for each director. &nbsp;Both incentive stock options and non-qualified stock options may be granted under the plan. &nbsp;Effective January 1, 2006, the Company adopted SFAS No. 123(R), <I>Share-Based Payment,</I> which requires that compensation cost relating to share-based payment transactions be recognized in the financial statements with measurement based upon the fair value of the equity or liability instruments issued.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The Plan was adopted by the Board of Directors of the Bank of Powhatan on May 8, 2001. &nbsp;This Plan was adopted by TransCommunity effective August 15, 2001 in connection with the Reorganization whereby the Bank of Powhatan became a subsidiary of TransCommunity. &nbsp;The purpose of the Plan is to reward employees and directors for services rendered and investment risks undertaken to date and to promote the success of TransCommunity and its subsidiaries by providing incentives to employees and directors that will promote the alignment of their personal financial interest with the long-term financial success of TransCommunity, its subsidiaries and with growth in shareholder value. The exercise price may not be less than 100% of the fair market value of the shares on the grant date. &nbsp;Unless the Stock Option Committee determines otherwise, one-third of a grant becomes vested and exercisable on each of the first three anniversaries of the initial grant date. &nbsp;Each grant becomes fully vested and exercisable in the event of a change in control of TransCommunity. &nbsp;All options are subject to exercise or forfeiture if TransCommunity&#146;s capital falls below its minimum requirements, as determined by its primary regulator, and TransCommunity&#146;s primary regulator so directs. The Plan will expire on May 7, 2011, unless terminated sooner by the Board of Directors. &nbsp;</P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.267px; margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:16.933px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16.933px"><B>NOTE 17</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.267px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px"><B>REGULATORY MATTERS:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.267px; margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Both TransCommunity and its subsidiaries are subject to various regulatory capital requirements administered by the federal banking agencies. &nbsp;If TransCommunity, or its subsidiary banks, fail to meet minimum capital requirements, its primary regulators can initiate certain mandatory and possible additional discretionary actions. &nbsp;If such actions are undertaken, they could have a direct material effect on TransCommunity&#146;s financial statements. Under capital adequacy guidelines and the regulatory framework for prompt corrective action, TransCommunity&#146;s subsidiary banks must meet specific capital guidelines that involve quantitative measures of each bank&#146;s assets, liabilities, and certain off-balance sheet items as calculated under regulatory accounting practices. &nbsp;Capital amounts and classification are also subject to qualitative judgments by the regulators about components, risk weightings, and other factors. &nbsp;Prompt corrective action provisions are not applicable to bank holding companies. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Quantitative measures are established by bank regulations to ensure capital adequacy. The Banks are required to maintain minimum amounts and ratios of total and Tier 1 capital (as defined in the regulations) to risk-weighted assets (as defined) and of Tier 1 capital (as defined) to average assets (as defined). &nbsp;At December 31, 2006 and 2005, management believes that the Company and the Banks met all capital adequacy requirements to which they are subject.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>

<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>TRANSCOMMUNITY FINANCIAL CORPORATION</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.067px; margin:0px" align=center><B>NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.267px; margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:16.933px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-16.933px"><B>NOTE 18</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.267px; margin:0px; text-indent:72px"><B>FAIR VALUE OF FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:15.733px; margin:0px"><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:6.667px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Statement of Financial Accounting Standards No. 107 (SFAS 107) &#147;<I>Disclosures About the Fair Value of Financial Statements</I>&#148; defines the fair value of a financial instrument as the amount at which a financial instrument could be exchanged in a current transaction between willing parties, other than in a forced liquidation sale. As the majority of the Banks&#146; financial instruments lack an available trading market, significant estimates, assumptions and present value calculations are required to determine estimated fair value.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Changes in the assumptions or methodologies used to estimate fair values may materially affect the estimated amounts. &nbsp;Also, management is concerned that there may not be reasonable comparability between the Company and other financial institutions due to the wide range of permitted assumptions and methodologies in the absence of active markets. &nbsp;This lack of uniformity gives rise to a high degree of subjectivity in estimating financial instrument fair values.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>TransCommunity has determined estimated fair values using the best available data and an estimation methodology suitable for each category of financial instruments. &nbsp;The estimation methodology used, the estimated fair values and the recorded carrying value of financial instruments at December 31, 2006 and 2005 are as follows:</P>

<P style="line-height:13.333px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>The estimated fair values of investment securities are based on quoted market prices if available or on the quoted market prices of comparable instruments if quoted market prices are not available. &nbsp;The gross loan portfolio and time deposits are valued using a present value discounted cash flow method where market prices are not available. &nbsp;The discount rate used in these calculations is the estimated current market rate adjusted for credit risk. &nbsp;All other financial instruments have fair values that approximate the carrying value.</P>

<B>NOTE 19 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS WITH OFF-BALANCE SHEET RISK:</B></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; text-indent:-96px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>In the normal course of business, the banks have outstanding commitments and contingent liabilities, such as commitments to extend credit and standby letters of credit, which are not included in the accompanying consolidated financial statements. &nbsp;The banks' exposure to credit loss in the event of nonperformance by the other party to the financial instruments for commitments to extend credit and standby letters of credit is represented by the contractual or notional amount of those instruments. &nbsp;The banks use the same credit policies in making such commitments as it does for instruments that are included in the consolidated balance sheets. &nbsp;</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px; text-indent:24px" align=justify>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</P>

<P style="line-height:13.333px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Commitments to extend credit are agreements to lend to a customer as long as there is no violation of any condition established in the contract. &nbsp;Commitments generally have fixed expiration dates or other termination clauses and may require payment of a fee. &nbsp;Since many of the commitments are expected to expire without being drawn upon, the total commitment amounts do not necessarily represent future cash requirements. &nbsp;The banks evaluate each customer's creditworthiness on a case-by-case basis. &nbsp;The amount of collateral obtained, if deemed necessary by the banks upon extension of credit, is based on management's credit evaluation. &nbsp;Collateral held varies but may include accounts receivable, inventory, property and equipment, and income-producing commercial properties.</P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:14.667px; margin:0px; padding-left:72px" align=justify>Standby letters of credit are conditional commitments issued by the banks to guarantee the performance of a customer to a third party. &nbsp;Standby letters of credit generally have fixed expiration dates or other termination clauses and may require payment of a fee. &nbsp;The credit risk involved in issuing letters of credit is essentially the same as that involved in extending loan facilities to customers. &nbsp;The banks' policy for obtaining collateral, and the nature of such collateral, is essentially the same as that involved in making commitments to extend credit.</P>
<P style="line-height:15.467px; margin:0px" align=justify><BR></P>
<P style="line-height:18.133px; margin-top:0px; margin-bottom:-18.133px" align=justify><B>NOTE 20</B></P>
